payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Afghanistan’s last decade has seen a decisive shift from a U.S.-backed Islamic Republic to Taliban governance following the 2021 withdrawal, with the United States completing its exit on August 30, 2021; the collapse of the former government and rapid Taliban gains marked a turning point in Afghan politics and security. The Taliban have sought to establish legitimacy while facing persistent insurgency pressures, limited international recognition, and ongoing security challenges across much of the countryside. Socially, the country has experienced tightened rights for women and civil society actors alongside a humanitarian and economic crisis as aid and development programs contracted or reoriented under new leadership. Economically, Afghanistan has faced sharp disruptions from conflict and Covid-19, with some signs of limited recovery supported by stabilization efforts and donor financing, yet remains heavily dependent on aid and informal economic activity. Internationally, Afghanistan’s position has been reshaped by ongoing diplomacy, neighboring state interests, and concerns over governance, security, and human rights, with major partners reassessing engagement and aid in a fraught environment.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: From 2016 to the present, Albania’s political reform trajectory has centered on strengthening the rule of law and anti-corruption institutions, with major milestones including ongoing judiciary reform, the vetting process for judges, and institutionalization of specialized anti-corruption bodies as Albania pushed EU accession talks starting in October 2024; these reforms have progressed alongside increased international scrutiny and conditionality from the EU, NATO, and regional partners. The security landscape has shifted toward deeper integration with Western institutions, marked by Albania’s continued alignment with EU foreign policy positions, expansion of defense modernization, and strengthened regional cooperation within the Western Balkans and NATO frameworks. Socially, the country has seen sustained efforts to modernize governance and public services, though concerns about corruption, governance capacity, and media pluralism persist amid political contestation; social development has benefited from targeted welfare spending and digitization efforts. Economically, growth has been supported by tourism, energy, and construction, while remittances and structural reforms underscore a transitional economy that seeks broader private-sector development and investment; governance reforms and closer EU integration are central to Albania’s development narrative as viewed in EU and international assessments. Albania’s international positioning remains anchored in EU accession hopes, active regional diplomacy, and commitment to rule-of-law reform, while adjusting expectations for reform pace against EU scrutiny and the broader Western Balkans reform agenda.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: From 2019 onward, Algeria’s Hirak protests forced the resignation of long-time president Bouteflika and catalyzed a constitutional reform path under Tebboune that maintained strong military influence while seeking civilian-led governance. The security landscape remained dominated by the army and security services, with authorities balancing repression of street protests against a rhetoric of reform, a dynamic underscored by international observers and human rights groups. Socially, mass demonstrations and civil-society activism persisted beyond the initial upheaval, even as public space for dissent faced restrictions and detainees were occasionally released in signals of reform. Economically, the state pursued diversification and private-sector-led growth amid ongoing dependence on hydrocarbons, with reforms and data-driven policy initiatives aimed at improving transparency, investment, and non-oil exports noted by the World Bank and IMF. Internationally, Algeria sought to recalibrate its partnerships and image by emphasizing diversified growth and regional diplomacy, while navigating external financial and policy advice to support a more open, albeit cautiously managed, development path.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since taking office in 2017, João Lourenço’s MPLA government pursued cautious reforms to consolidate stability after dos Santos and secured a renewed mandate in the 2022 elections, albeit with a substantially narrower majority. Security and governance have seen a mixture of tariffed liberalization and periodic constraints on civil liberties, as Angola’s political space remained tightly managed even as opposition coalitions persisted ahead of 2022. Social change has been shaped by persistent youth disillusionment and limited room for broad-based protests, even as urban areas pressed for jobs and services. Economically, Angola has pressed reforms to diversify beyond oil, supported by IMF-driven fiscal governance measures and a National Development Plan aimed at non-oil growth, though oil still dominates revenues and export composition. Internationally, the country has sought external support for macro stability and diversification, engaging with multilateral partners and pursuing a debt-sustainability path through IMF programs and related reforms.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, Antarctica’s governance has remained anchored in the Antarctic Treaty System, which emphasizes peaceful scientific activity and bans military use while keeping sovereignty claims non-enforceable; the system has continued to adapt through review processes and Ministerial Declarations by Consultative Parties, reinforcing the mining ban and environmental protections. Security considerations have largely centered on safeguarding the continent’s pristine environment and monitoring unauthorized activities, with recent analyses stressing compliance, surveillance, and cooperative law enforcement under the CEP and related measures. Social and scientific development has grown around international collaborations, open data, and capacity-building within a growing community of researchers and polar programs, though policy debates remain outside the continent itself due to its non-sovereign status. Economic development remains understated by design, prioritizing research infrastructure and tourism governance within strict environmental rules rather than traditional growth metrics; the growth of Antarctic science and industry is framed within the Madrid Protocol’s Environmental Protection regime and ongoing ATS reforms to accommodate climate research and logistical needs. International positioning has solidified around multilateral leadership by Antarctic Treaty Consultative Parties, with calls for stronger governance mechanisms and updates to the Secretariat’s role to manage a changing governance landscape, as highlighted by recent academic and policy analyses of ATS evolution.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Argentina’s last decade has seen a political pivot from the Kirchner era to Mauricio Macri’s market-oriented government (2015–2019) and then a return to Peronist leadership under Alberto Fernández (from 2019 onward), with continued emphasis on foreign policy realignment and debt management. Macri’s term pursued deregulation and openness to markets but faced repeated debt strains, drought-related shocks, and high inflation, contributing to his 2019 electoral defeat. Fernández inherited a deeply indebted, inflation-prone economy and led negotiations to renegotiate external debt and secure IMF support while seeking to broaden social protection and stabilize macroeconomics. The COVID-19 pandemic intensified economic strain and prompted lockdowns, highlighting social safety nets and political fault lines over policy direction and fiscal sustainability. Internationally, Argentina has sought to balance relations with regional neighbors, maintain engagement with traditional partners, and navigate global financial pressures while projecting a more collaborative stance on debt and development.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Armenia’s recent history has been shaped by the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh ceasefire brokered by Russia, which ended the 2020 war and led to redraws around the region; in the following years Armenia pursued greater international engagement even as security concerns remained, including European and Western diplomacy to support border management and regional stability. The country achieved a notable governance and development milestone by joining the World Bank’s IDA framework in 2023, signaling a push toward development-focused reforms and stronger international financial ties. In 2023 and 2024, Armenia faced a significant humanitarian and logistical challenge as the Lachin Corridor blockade affected Nagorno-Karabakh, drawing international attention to the region’s humanitarian situation and the fragility of the ceasefire. The IMF’s 2024 program reviews underscored fiscal consolidation and structural reforms to sustain macro stability, while still aiming to support social spending, infrastructure, and healthcare modernization. Overall, Armenia’s trajectory over the past decade reflects a balance between security pressures, incremental institutional reform, and efforts to diversify its international economic and political partnerships.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: In the last decade, Australia’s political scene shifted toward greater policy activism after May 2022 when Anthony Albanese became prime minister and signaled a focus on climate action, social policy, and economic reform. Canberra’s security posture intensified, reinforcing the US alliance and adopting an assertive Indo-Pacific stance that includes the AUKUS nuclear-submarine arrangement and broader defense cooperation with regional partners. Social policy evolved with reforms in climate governance and migration, reflecting a push toward decarbonisation and social inclusion under a more reform-minded agenda. Economically, Australia pursued diversification and supply-chain security, balancing trade with China while embracing Indo-Pacific economic initiatives to strengthen regional resilience. Internationally, it positioned itself as a leading Indo-Pacific democracy, expanding partnerships with the EU and India and shaping regional rules through multi-laceted diplomacy and defense cooperation.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: From 2017, Austria's political trajectory was reshaped when Chancellor Sebastian Kurz's ÖVP formed a coalition with the far-right FP0, a partnership that unsettled the European mainstream before the Ibiza affair precipitated a 2019 collapse of the government and snap elections; after that crisis Kurz returned to power in a 2020 coalition with the Greens, marking a rare center-right/center-left government in Vienna; security and social debates intensified around migration policy and rule-of-law scrutiny, with investigations and political scandals shaping public trust; economically, Austria emphasized stability and social peace while pursuing energy transition and climate policy within EU frameworks, supported by European commissions' guidance and IEA framing; internationally, the country has balanced deeper EU integration with its traditional neutrality and domestic legal probes around Kurz that continued to keep Austria in European political discourse.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Azerbaijan over the past decade has consolidated a centralized political system under President Ilham Aliyev while deepening security ties with Turkey and Russia in the wake of the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war. The security landscape has shifted to include a Russian-Turkish-influenced postwar order, with Azerbaijan regaining control of Nagorno-Karabakh in 2020 and facing subsequent regional pressures and ceasefire dynamics through 2023. Socially, the state has emphasized national unity and security narratives, alongside displacement and governance constraints that shape public discourse. Economically, Baku has pursued postwar reconstruction and diversification of energy-related investments, though growth remains bound to energy markets and external partnerships rather than broad-based social mobility. Internationally, Azerbaijan has positioned itself as a regional power balancing Ankara, Moscow, and Western partners, while pursuing normalization with Armenia and attracting investment through its strategic role in the South Caucasus.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: The Bahamas has experienced a notable political shift since the 2017 general election, with the Free National Movement taking office and guiding policy through a new administration within a stable parliamentary framework. The security and resilience of the state were tested by the 2019 Hurricane Dorian and the 2020 pandemic, which together strained public finances and underscored the need for disaster readiness and social support, according to regional development analyses. Social change has featured active advocacy on human rights and gender equality within the CARICOM community, boosting regional dialogue even as domestic debates continue on issues such as gender and rights protections. Economically, the country remains heavily dependent on tourism and financial services, while the government pursues diversification into digital and blue economies and infrastructure improvements to strengthen resilience and inclusive growth. International positioning has reinforced Bahamas’ role in CARICOM and regional security dialogues, with ongoing engagement in hemispheric forums like the OAS and continued emphasis on regional cooperation and policy alignment.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, Bangladesh’s political landscape has been dominated by the ruling Awami League, which won the 2018 general election amid strong opposition objections and has faced ongoing domestic protests and calls for greater electoral openness into the mid-2020s. The Rohingya refugee crisis, triggered by violence in Myanmar in 2017, has profoundly shaped security and humanitarian policies, making Bangladesh the host of what authorities and observers describe as a large, precarious refugee situation with evolving camp security concerns. Economically, the ready-made garment sector remains central to growth and jobs while facing global shifts, energy-transition pressures, and pandemic-era disruptions that highlighted the need for resilience and social sustainability beyond headline GDP figures. Socially, Bangladesh has pursued sustained development gains—particularly in female labor participation and poverty reduction linked to export-led growth—while grappling with labor conditions, climate risks, and urban challenges that require ongoing policy attention. Internationally, Dhaka has sought to diversify ties with India, China, and Western partners, navigating regional security dynamics and seeking support for humanitarian and development needs through multilateral channels.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, Belarus has consolidated authoritarian control under President Alexander Lukashenko, with the 2020 presidential election triggering unprecedented mass protests and a sustained crackdown on civil society and dissent. Security services intensified surveillance and repression of journalists and opposition figures, eroding domestic political space even as some detainees were periodically released, reflecting a mixed pattern of coercion and selective tactical concessions. The economy faced sanctions and external pressures, contributing to stagflation and shifts in trade patterns while Minsk deepened economic ties with Moscow and faced currency and inflationary pressures. Social and labor dynamics shifted as independent unions and protest movements sought rights and democratic norms, often at great personal risk to activists and organizers. Internationally, Belarus has drifted into a tighter orbit with Russia while facing persistent EU and Western criticism and limited engagement on human rights, sanctions, and security cooperation, with policy debates about re-engagement continuing into the mid-2020s.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade Belgium’s federal landscape has remained coalition-driven, with governance navigated by a five‑party arrangement that has sought policy continuity despite regional fault lines and occasional stalemates, culminating in a new government formed in February 2025 under Prime Minister Bart De Wever. Security, policing and justice surfaced as top priorities in the federal agenda, including proposals to unify Brussels’ police services and to strengthen measures against extremist rhetoric and violence. Migration and asylum policy moved toward tighter controls, following a 2017 asylum reform and continued reform discussions culminating in a 2023 Migration Deal that sparked debate over reception, asylum procedures and family reunification. Social policy and integration continued to be shaped by capacity challenges in housing asylum seekers and ongoing debates over how best to balance protection with social welfare and integration obligations. Economically, Belgium emphasized stable development and social protection within a highly federal framework, with emphasis on leveraging regional autonomy while maintaining national coordination on key security and migration issues.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade Belize has pursued a more assertive regional role while navigating domestic security challenges, including persistent gang violence and crime that remain a domestic priority. The government rolled out new cybersecurity and digital-government initiatives to bolster resilience amid evolving threats. Belize has faced governance concerns and corruption perceptions, even as institutions work with international partners on AML/CFT and security reforms. Economically, tourism and services recovered post-pandemic with growth but the country continues to balance debt and investment needs with social development. On the international stage Belize has strengthened ties within CARICOM and regional diplomacy, while dealing with border questions and migration policies.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since Patrice Talon took office in 2016 he has steered Benin through a reform-driven economic opening and anti-corruption push, while observers note that political power has become more centralized and parliamentary checks have faced strain. Security near Benin’s northern frontier has intensified regional risks, including jihadist spillovers and a 2022 attack at W National Park, prompting strengthened border and policing cooperation with neighbors and international partners. Social policy has prioritized human capital and social spending, contributing to improvements in health, education and living standards even as gains remain uneven across the population. The economy has blended private‑sector reform with resilient public investment, marked by a 2019 Eurobond, IMF program support, and continued diversification under Minister Wadagni, while external lenders have raised Benin’s profile in international markets. diplomatically, Benin has sought to balance relations with regional neighbors, France and other traditional partners while leveraging its status as a relatively stable democracy in West Africa to attract investment and development assistance.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Bhutan’s political system shifted from an absolute monarchy to a constitutional framework with competitive elections and a functioning parliament beginning in 2008, marking a definitive democratic transition over the past decade; its security and governance remain tightly linked to India, even as it seeks a more balanced regional posture and border talks with China. The country has faced social and development pressures—from climate vulnerability to the COVID-19 pandemic—while reporting progress in health and human development and managing vulnerability tied to hydropower revenues. Economically, Bhutan pursued diversification beyond hydropower through digitalization and e-trade initiatives to boost resilience and inclusive growth, even as growth remained modest and external shocks affected performance. Internationally, Bhutan has backed long‑term economic and development roadmaps—such as the 10X National Economic Vision and UNDP‑supported plans—to climb toward higher income levels while prioritizing environmental sustainability and careful management of its delicate balance with major neighbors.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Bolivia’s 2019 political crisis ended Evo Morales’s presidency with Jeanine Áñez’s self‑declared interim government, a period marked by violent protests and international debate over legitimacy and rights, which drew condemnation from human rights groups. In November 2020 Luis Arce of MAS was elected president, signaling a return to Morales‑era economic policies and a push to restore governance after the turbulent transition. Security and judicial concerns persisted, including contentious prosecutions and human rights critiques of the interim period, which continued to shape Bolivia’s legal and political climate into the mid‑2020s. Economically, the Arce administration has pursued diversification beyond hydrocarbons, emphasized gas sector stabilization, and sought to build a Bolivian lithium industry through state involvement and foreign partnerships, while facing delays and domestic debate over industrialization goals. Internationally, Bolivia has sought to re‑position itself through energy strategy and regional diplomacy, balancing domestic resource nationalism with engagement in global markets and partnerships around lithium, gas, and energy security.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Bosnia and Herzegovina submitted a formal request for EU membership in 2016 and won candidate status in 2022, setting a path toward gradual alignment with EU norms despite ongoing internal deadlock among its ethnic groups, and in 2024 the EU signaled a green light to open accession talks contingent on reform progress. The security landscape has remained anchored by the EU-led stabilization mission and the ongoing presence of EUFOR Althea, with international actors pressuring for rule-of-law and reform while warning against renewed instability. Socially, the country has seen persistent protests and civil society advocacy around governance, anti-corruption, and constitutional reform, even as political elites grapple with the country’s complex power-sharing structure. Economically, BiH has pursued reforms through EU-backed programs and reform plans, but implementation has been uneven, with external support like the Reform and Growth Facility linked to cautious domestic absorption and domestic implementation challenges. Internationally, BiH has pursued deeper ties with the EU and Western allies, while balancing relations with neighbors and maintaining a reform agenda amid concerns about legitimacy and governance at the state, entity, and cantonal levels.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade Botswana has navigated change from Masisi's rise in 2018 amid tensions with former president Khama, steering a presidency focused on reform and governance. The 2024 elections marked a historic shift as the Umbrella for Democratic Change defeated the long-dominant Botswana Democratic Party, bringing Duma Boko to the presidency and signaling a more competitive party system. Security and civil liberties faced scrutiny under debates over institutions and dissent, with international observers noting strengthening democratic practices but concerns about executive leverage. Economically, Botswana continued its diversification efforts through Vision 2036 frameworks and UN/development-backed diversification strategies, while the diamond downturn pressured revenues and spurred diversification plans. Internationally, Botswana maintained a steady regional voice in SADC and pursued inclusive growth partnerships, even as it reassessed development priorities after the 2024 electoral shift.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Brazil’s political trajectory shifted from the Dilma Rousseff impeachment and a turbulent Temer presidency (2016–2018) to Jair Bolsonaro’s right‑wing administration (2019–2022) marked by market‑friendly reforms yet deep social and political polarization. In 2023 Lula da Silva returned to the presidency, moving quickly to revoke or modify Bolsonaro policies, expand social programs, and restore a more interventionist stance on the Amazon and public security with a restructured federal administration. The security and justice landscape has seen ongoing debates over police practices, gun control, and public safety, alongside efforts to strengthen environmental protections and Amazon governance under Lula’s leadership. Economically, Brazil weathered a long recession aftermath, pursued tax reform and social spending recalibration, and faced a cautious but improving growth path with a focus on job creation and social inclusion, while its development agenda tied to infrastructure and regional integration progressed unevenly. Internationally, Brazil has sought to reclaim a leadership role on the world stage, reengaging with multilateral forums, promoting climate and biodiversity agendas, and positioning itself within BRICS and the global economy amid shifting geopolitical dynamics.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade Brunei has remained an absolute monarchy under Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah while pursuing cautious modernization and economic planning through Wawasan 2035 to diversify beyond oil and gas. The security and foreign-policy posture has emphasized regional stability and a careful balancing of ASEAN alignments, maintaining internal harmony and limited political liberalization in practice. Social policy gained global attention in 2019 with the phased implementation of Sharia penal codes, including harsh punishments for LGBT acts and adultery, which drew international condemnation and later a moratorium on the most severe penalties. Economically Brunei has pressed downstream and non-oil sectors as part of diversification efforts, with modest growth in non-oil activity and ongoing investment in sectors like food, services, tourism, and ICT. International positioning has focused on maintaining strong ties with neighbors and partners in Asia while seeking to attract investment and technology transfer through public-private initiatives, even as it preserves conservative domestic governance and royal prerogatives.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, Bulgaria’s politics have been defined by a cycle of protests and caretaker governments challenging entrenched oligarchic influence, culminating in a 2023 coalition and a 2024 political crisis that tested stability and reform pledges, including anti-corruption measures and constitutional changes aimed at weakening presidential influence over security and intelligence services, though progress remained uneven. The security dimension has grown as Bulgaria reinforced its role in NATO’s eastern flank, hosting multinational battlegroups and pledging defense spending to bolster regional deterrence amid the broader Ukraine conflict (with high-level visits and military exercises highlighting the alliance’s focus on Black Sea security). Socially, widespread protests from 2020 onward reflected public frustration with corruption, governance gaps, and the cost of living, while civil society and media groups pressed for transparency and rule-of-law reforms; these pressures intersected with political shifts as new and reconfigured parties emerged. Economically, Bulgaria faced headwinds from EU fund absorption challenges and governance bottlenecks that constrained recovery plan implementation, even as the EU and international partners pledged support through funds and structural programmes to modernize infrastructure and the blue economy context in line with the 2021-2027 partnership agreements. Internationally, Bulgaria has sought to balance its EU and NATO commitments with regional diplomacy, aiming to advance euro adoption and Schengen integration while navigating complex relations with Russia and competing domestic narratives about reform and resilience. payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2015 Burkina Faso has faced a deepening Islamist insurgency that has driven displacement, humanitarian needs, and a persistent security challenge across the Sahel, complicating governance and development. A string of military coups from 2022—Damiba's initial seizure in January and his overthrow in September by Traoré—has left the country under a junta that has pursued security-focused policies while straining relations with ECOWAS and some Western partners. International responses have included regional pressure, suspended memberships, and varied levels of engagement with aid programmes as the state struggles to stabilize fighting between security forces and insurgent groups. The IMF and World Bank have continued conditional support and analysis, stressing that growth must translate into broader social gains amid ongoing conflict and climate-related development constraints. Human rights investigations in 2026 have highlighted abuses by both security forces and armed groups, underscoring the difficult path toward civilian rule and accountability while humanitarian needs remain acute.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Burundi’s last decade has been defined by a sharp narrowing of political space following the 2015 crisis, with the ruling CNDD-FDD tightening control and electricitying crackdowns on dissent amid protests and international scrutiny. The 2020 elections marked a formal transition to President Evariste Ndayishimiye, but security forces and imbonerakure-aligned actions continued to target opponents, journalists and civil society, generating ongoing allegations of arrests, disappearances and trials lack of due process. Human rights organizations repeatedly warned that abuses persisted in 2019–2021 and beyond, including restrictions on media, assembly and political opposition, even as some state actors pursued reconciliation rhetoric; the UN COI’s findings and subsequent reporting highlighted persistent impunity and legal constraints. Economically, Burundi has pursued development and public-works priorities under a government-led agenda, while a large portion of the population remains vulnerable to poverty, displacement and reliance on regional trade and aid networks, with the CNDD-FDD maintaining intra-state leverage over security and institutions. Internationally, Burundi has navigated a complex position—engaging with regional bodies and donors while facing scrutiny from human rights bodies and, earlier, an ICC investigation into crimes against humanity—yet its policy direction continues to center on regime durability and security concerns rather than broad civic liberalization.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Cambodia’s political landscape shifted decisively in 2023 when Hun Manet, long groomed as Hun Sen’s successor, was installed as prime minister after a 2018- and 2023-election environment widely criticized as one-sided, signaling a generational transition within the CPP; the leadership change has been paired with continued constraints on opposition parties and civil society. Amnesty International and rights observers have documented a sustained crackdown on media, NGOs and dissent since the run-up to the 2018 elections, with limited space for independent voices persisting into the 2020s. Socially, the country has seen ongoing struggles over rights and livelihoods, including activist detentions and later procedural releases amid broader governance concerns, while environmental and labor issues remain contentious in the context of rapid development. Economically, Cambodia has leaned on foreign investment and Chinese development finance to bolster infrastructure and manufacturing, alongside a diversified but export-reliant garment sector, shaping a growth model tightly linked with external partners. Regionally and internationally, Cambodia has pursued a policy of cautious neutrality within ASEAN and has positioned itself to leverage relations with major powers, balancing close ties with China while maintaining engagement with traditional partners and regional forums.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since late 2016, the Anglophone crisis in Cameroon’s Northwest and Southwest has evolved from peaceful protests over language and governance into an ongoing armed conflict with widespread civilian casualties and displacement, a trajectory documented by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, and parliamentary briefings. The Biya government has pursued a centralized, long-dominant political path and intensified counter-insurgency operations in the English-speaking regions, while space for opposition and independent media has narrowed. Social and humanitarian impacts have included disruptions to schooling, increases in displacement, and ongoing rights concerns raised by international observers. Economically, Cameroon has continued to pursue diversification and development projects, but security costs and governance questions have limited broad, sustained improvements beyond headline growth figures. Internationally, Yaoundé has sought engagement with Western partners and regional bodies, balancing relations with France and other powers while facing periodic mediation efforts and scrutiny over rights and humanitarian access.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since the 2015 federal election, Canada’s Liberal government under Justin Trudeau has pursued a policy agenda that centers climate action, Indigenous reconciliation, and a more active role in global institutions. Security and defence have been recalibrated toward NORAD modernization and a more assertive alignment with allies, even as Ottawa navigated a substantively challenging Canada–China relationship and broader Indo-Pacific dynamics. Social change has been a core driver, with commitments to gender equality, diversity, and implementing Truth and Reconciliation Commission calls to action plus measures addressing Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls. Economically, Canada has sought trade diversification and a cleaner energy transition, while advancing policies on critical minerals, supply-chain resilience, and sustainable development beyond GDP focus. International positioning has emphasized open diplomacy with allies, a nuanced stance toward China, and renewed engagement in Arctic governance, multilateral security, and North American cooperation.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, Faustin-Archange Touadéra's 2016 election steered CAR toward political continuity after the 2013 crisis, even as the state struggled to extend governance beyond Bangui. A 2019 peace agreement between the government and 14 armed groups provided a framework for disarmament and stabilization, though its implementation has remained uneven and fragile. International peacekeeping, notably MINUSCA, and regional security initiatives continued to underpin efforts, even as sporadic violence and rebel attacks persisted. Russia-backed Wagner forces figured prominently in security dynamics, influencing both operations and international perceptions of the conflict. By late 2025 and into 2026, elections were held in relatively calmer conditions with observers noting a more peaceful environment and Touadéra securing a renewed mandate amid ongoing security challenges.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: From 2016 onward Chad faced persistent security pressures from jihadist groups across the Sahel, with regional forces and French involvement shaping military operations, until the 2021 death of President Idriss Deby Itno on the battlefield and the subsequent establishment of a Transitional Military Council led by his son, Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno. The 18‑month transition stretched into years as authorities pursued a roadmap toward elections while navigating protests and domestic and regional unrest, including the ongoing fight against insurgents like Boko Haram and IS‑affiliated groups. Economically, oil-driven growth has fluctuated, prompting international lenders to urge diversification and governance reforms even as 2023 growth rose to about 4–5% before materializing in later years amid floods and external shocks; Sudan’s 2023–24 refugee surge also pressed public spending and social services. Social and humanitarian pressures intensified with the Sudan crisis and climate–related shocks, pushing Chad to host a growing refugee population while international partners emphasized inclusive public investment and private‑sector development to reduce vulnerability. Internationally, Chad has remained a key Sahel security partner and beneficiary of donor support and debt restructuring, balancing engagement with Western partners and regional initiatives while seeking a clearer path to civilian governance through ongoing electoral planning and transition milestones.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, Chile’s politics were jolted by the 2019-2020 protests that spotlighted inequality and culminated in a 2020 national plebiscite backing a process to draft a new constitution. The subsequent constitutional journey, including a 2021-2022 Constitutional Convention, produced a progressive draft that was ultimately rejected in a 2022 referendum, shaping a era of recalibrated expectations about reform and governance. In national leadership, Gabriel Boric’s 2022-2026 presidency embodied a generation-shift in Chilean politics, pursuing social inclusion and regulatory changes while navigating inflation and embedded market concerns. On the economy, Chile continued to rely on copper and mining, balancing social pressure for redistribution with a commodity-driven growth model and fiscal constraints, amid evolving international trade dynamics. Internationally, Chile sought to position itself as a stable regional partner within Latin America’s evolving left-right mix, while engaging in regional blocs and trade links that extend beyond its traditional ties to the United States and neighboring economies.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since Xi Jinping consolidated power after 2012, he restructured party and state institutions to tighten top-level control, culminating in a 2022 constitutional change that allowed him a third term as paramount leader, signaling a durable leadership trajectory. The security and political sphere have grown more centralized, with Beijing extending its reach over Hong Kong through the 2020 national security law and sustained censorship and surveillance, intensifying controls on dissent and media. Human rights concerns persist in Xinjiang and Hong Kong, drawing ongoing international scrutiny as authorities defend policies in counterterrorism and social stability while critics raise allegations of abuses. Economically, China has pushed for technological self-reliance and a new dual-circulation development framework under the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021–2025) to steer growth, investment, and innovation while seeking greater resilience amid external pressures and a more assertive international posture through initiatives like the Belt and Road. Internationally, Beijing has positioned itself as a more influential, sometimes adversarial, actor in global governance, trade, and security, balancing strategic partnerships with rivals as it expands its influence across Asia, Africa, and beyond while resisting Western pressure on human rights and national sovereignty.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2022, President Gustavo Petro’s Paz Total approach marks a shift toward negotiated settlements with illegal armed groups and a security strategy that mixes dialogue with targeted pressure; the government frames this as a move to end decades of conflict through broad participation and reforms. The 2016 peace accord with FARC remains central to security policy, but disarmament timelines and dissident groups have complicated full implementation, while clashes and violence in places like Antioquia and the southwest illustrate a fragile security landscape. Socially, Colombia pursues more inclusive spending and regional development to reduce inequality, though observers warn that informality, regional gaps, and ambitious reform fatigue could slow progress. Economically, growth has been modest and investment uneven, with reform agendas aiming to raise fiscal capacity and public efficiency while external outlooks flag volatility and persistent productivity challenges. Internationally, Colombia has sought to position itself as a reform-minded regional actor, balancing U.S. security cooperation with a social-justice oriented governance agenda and engaging multiple partners to support peace and development efforts.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since winning a contested third term in 2016, President Denis Sassou Nguesso has consolidated power through a mix of political control and selective reforms, underscoring the long-standing dominance of his party in the Republic of the Congo; in parallel, international observers have repeatedly raised concerns about electoral fairness and restrictions on opposition voices. Security in the Pool region and other areas has remained fragile, with security forces crackdowns and occasional violence amid protests and rebel activity, while the country has continued to contribute to regional peacekeeping efforts in Central Africa. Social change has progressed unevenly, with continued focus on education, health, and social protection programs supported by international partners, even as social indicators lag behind some regional peers; civil society and independent media continue to face pressure, according to rights assessments, even as some development projects expand access to basic services. The economy has pursued diversification beyond oil through new public investments and digital/infra initiatives guided by a 2022–2026 national plan, but growth remains constrained by structural fragility and external shocks, with the government engaging multilateral institutions to finance and steer reform. Internationally, Congo-Brazzaville has maintained close ties with France, sought to elevate its regional role in the Central African Republic and beyond, and aligned with regional security frameworks while balancing engagement with global partners and financial institutions.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since taking office in 2022, President Rodrigo Chaves pursued a more confrontational style that challenged established parties and institutions, marking a shift in Costa Rica’s political dynamics. Security and crime have dominated public debate, with rising homicide levels and debates over how to balance civil liberties with public safety in a country long famed for stability. Civil society and independent media have faced renewed pressure and polarization has intensified, even as women’s representation rose in the 2026 electoral cycle and parliamentary composition shifted toward greater gender balance. The economy remains service- and tourism-led, with growing tech-enabled sectors like medical devices, though public service delays and governance challenges continue to prompt calls for reform and greater institutional efficiency. Internationally, Costa Rica has continued to promote democratic norms and regional leadership while navigating a changing Central American security landscape, as the 2026 election introduced Laura Fernández Delgado as a new executive mandate with potential implications for policy direction and checks-and-balances.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the last decade Croatia deepened its integration with the European Union by adopting the euro and joining the Schengen Area on January 1, 2023, marking a major step in its EU membership trajectory. Politically, since 2016 the government led by the HDZ under Prime Minister Andrej Plenković pursued European alignment and reform agendas, even as EU rule-of-law concerns about judiciary and media independence persisted. In security and international positioning, Croatia remained a stable NATO member, reinforcing regional security cooperation and leveraging EU frameworks for modernization and cross-border governance within Schengen. Socially, public debate has focused on media freedom, pluralism, and reform implementation, including legislative steps around the European Media Freedom Act and related transparency measures. Economically, Croatia benefited from EU funds for development and reform, with notable milestones such as euro adoption and ESM eligibility strengthening its integration and financial resilience beyond GDP growth figures.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Cuba’s last decade has seen a formal shift from Raúl Castro’s leadership to Miguel Díaz-Canel, with Díaz-Canel taking consolidated command by 2021 while the Communist Party maintained tight political control; the transition has been gradual rather than abrupt, emphasizing continuity in the revolutionary framework. Security remained vigilant with continued state surveillance and occasional crackdowns on dissent, even as economic reforms sought to liberalize some aspects of daily life. Social change included formal advances on gender and sexual orientation rights in the 2019 constitution and related reforms, even as daily life continued to face shortages, inflation, and constraints on political expression. Economically, Cuba pursued a long-term update of its socialist model beginning in 2011, highlighted by the 2021 monetary reform that exposed currency weaknesses and accelerated partial dollarization in practice. Internationally, Havana has recalibrated its relations with the United States and the European Union while sustaining long-standing ties with allies like Venezuela, as sanctions pressure and shifting oil dynamics shaped its external posture by the mid-2020s.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Cyprus has pursued closer Western alignment and EU integration while managing ongoing division and security challenges, including increased EU-focused diplomacy as it prepared for and hosted EU Council presidency activities in early 2026. The country has continued to engage in complex energy diplomacy over eastern Mediterranean gas reserves, balancing exploration promises with Turkish objections and broader regional tensions. Migration and asylum policy remained a domestic and political issue, with reforms and reception-management challenges influencing social and political debate through the mid-2020s. Economically, Cyprus weathered post-pandemic pressures with structural reforms and investment oversight, highlighting resilience and diversification beyond tourism and real estate. Internationally, Cyprus emphasized its EU role, Schengen accession prospects, and a more assertive stance within regional security discussions, while the Cyprus question persisted in UN and EU forums as talks toward reunification remained stalled.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: From 2017 to 2021, Czech politics were dominated by Andrej Babiš and the populist ANO movement, steering a minority government that relied on coalition partners and later fell under a broader reform agenda after the 2021 elections; since then, political leadership has swung between pro-European, pro-reform coalitions and a controversial return of ANO leadership by 2025–26. The security posture hardened in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, with Prague aligning closely with NATO and EU partners and supporting Ukraine while balancing national defense and regional deterrence. Domestically, the country has faced social and economic pressures around housing affordability, energy security, and the pace of the energy transition, even as EU funding and green investments shape infrastructure and industry. Economically, the Czech Republic has leveraged EU financing, including near-€2 billion from the EIB Group in 2025 for rail, grids, and housing, as well as ongoing reform programs tied to energy and security cooperation. Internationally, Prague’s stance has evolved with leadership changes—shifting between Euro-enthusiasm and occasional Euro-skeptic signals as new coalitions form—while continuing to participate actively in EU and NATO agendas and maintaining some degrees of strategic independence.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since the 2011 post-election crisis, Côte d'Ivoire has experienced political stabilization under President Alassane Ouattara, though the 2016 constitutional change resetting term limits and subsequent elections have kept the ruling coalition dominant and opposition space limited. Security has improved overall, with international partners helping to wind down peacekeeping while electoral periods occasionally provoke unrest and wider concerns about political rights. Social change has included targeted social protection and employment programs aimed at youth, alongside efforts to expand access to basic services as the state seeks broader inclusion. The economy has diversified away from a sole reliance on cocoa and agriculture toward infrastructure and services, supported by successive national development plans and sustained growth, even as the country remains vulnerable to commodity cycles and climate risks. Internationally, Ivory Coast has positioned itself as a regional stability and growth anchor, attracting investment and reinforcing ties with neighbors and development partners while reinforcing governance reforms to maintain its status as Africa’s de facto beacon of post-crisis recovery.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since Félix Tshisekedi took office in January 2019, the DRC has seen a fragile political consolidation with the ruling coalition expanding influence after contentious elections, though opposition and civil society flagged integrity concerns. Security in the eastern provinces has remained volatile, with battles involving the M23 and other armed groups causing displacement and humanitarian strain. The 2023 elections yielded a Tshisekedi-led government and parliamentary majority, but observers warned of irregularities and violence affecting trust in the process. The economy remains resource-rich but development proceeds unevenly amid conflict, governance challenges, and external influence over minerals and logistics. International actors, including MONUSCO, regional bodies, and major powers, have continued to push for peacekeeping, reform, and governance while balancing mineral security interests.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Denmark has pursued a more outward-facing security and defence posture since the mid-2010s, culminating in a broad 2023 defence framework that aims to meet NATO targets earlier and expand conscription with gender-equal, longer service. The country’s foreign policy has emphasised a balanced Atlantic-Nordic-European approach, strengthening NATO ties, deepening U.S. cooperation, and reconsidering EU defence roles in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Domestically, Denmark enacted an ambitious Climate Act in 2019 to accelerate its green transition, supported by substantial subsidies and cross-party public climate commitments through the subsequent decade. The government has also sought to manage migration and asylum policy through high-profile proposals and reshuffles, alongside defending welfare-state commitments in a changing European security environment. Internationally, Denmark has positioned itself as a key ally in European security and Arctic affairs, while navigating EU opt-out dynamics and ongoing debates about defence policy within both the EU and NATO frameworks.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2016, Djibouti has seen the long-serving president Ismaïl Omar Guelleh consolidate power while adapting constitutional rules to extend his rule, including a 2025 revision that removed a presidential age limit and broadened eligibility, paving the way for a potential sixth term in 2026. The country has maintained a security-forward posture as a hub for multiple foreign militaries and as a key partner in Red Sea security initiatives, reinforcing its strategic importance amid regional tensions. Socially, Djibouti has pursued social protection and inclusive growth within its development plans, even as urbanization continues and job creation remains a central challenge. Economically, growth has leaned on the country’s port services and transshipment activity as regional trade flows shift, with the state aiming to diversify beyond logistics and finance social outcomes like health and education. Djibouti’s international positioning reflects a dual strategy of anchoring strong security partnerships—particularly with the United States, China, and France—while leveraging port and logistical assets to attract regional investment and influence within the Horn of Africa and beyond.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: The Dominican Republic’s political scene shifted in 2020 when Luis Abinader of the Modern Revolutionary Party defeated the long-ruling PLD, signaling a new era after years of PLD governance. Since then, the government has pursued anti-corruption efforts while confronting ongoing concerns about security and human rights, including police-involved killings that led to detentions of officers in 2024–2025. Security officials have faced scrutiny over extrajudicial executions, prompting calls from civil society for independent investigations and greater accountability. Economically, the country has pushed diversification beyond tourism with a services-led growth path and structural reforms, though COVID-19 exposed weaknesses and underscored the need for more inclusive development and resilience. Internationally, the DR has maintained close ties with the United States, leveraged free zones and FDI to support development, and navigated regional security dynamics, including migration pressures related to Haiti.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade Ecuador moved from Rafael Correa’s long-running political project toward Lenín Moreno’s presidency (2017–2021) and then Guillermo Lasso’s administration (2021–2023), before the ascent of Daniel Noboa in late 2023, signaling a volatile but shifting political cycle. Security deteriorated markedly as organized crime and drug trafficking intensified, prompting multiple states of emergency and a high toll of violence that observers say places Ecuador among Latin America’s most dangerous countries by the mid‑2020s. Social policy and governance faced criticisms for rolling back some protections and for controversial decisions on resource allocation, governance practices, and vaccine access during the health crisis era. The economy remained challenged by debt, inflation, and structural reform debates, with the IMF and external lenders shaping policy space while social movements drove protests over living costs and public services. International positioning has leaned toward pragmatic security cooperation and regional alignments, even as domestic political upheavals complicated diplomatic consensus and Ecuador’s engagement with global partners.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: In 2013 Egypt experienced a military coup led by then-defense minister Abdel Fattah el-Sisi that unleashed a broad crackdown on dissent and dismantling of the Muslim Brotherhood, an episode that drew widespread rights concerns. Sisi then won the presidency in 2014 and has governed with a centralized, security-focused approach that many observers view as a rollback of previous democratic openings. In 2019 parliament amended the constitution to extend presidential terms and allow Sisi to remain in office through 2030, signaling a long-term consolidation of rule. Economically, Cairo pursued IMF-backed reforms after 2016, with a 2024 IMF augmentation underscoring ongoing macroeconomic challenges and a push to mobilize private-sector growth. Internationally, Egypt has deepened ties with Gulf partners and positioned itself as a regional stabilizer, even as rights groups warn of authoritarian tendencies and persistent domestic repression.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since taking office in 2019, President Nayib Bukele has prioritized a hard-edged anti-gang crackdown, deploying security forces and declaring a state of emergency that expanded police powers. This approach coincided with a dramatic drop in homicides through 2024, though critics warn it relied on mass arrests and raised due-process concerns. In 2021 El Salvador became the first country to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender, a move that drew international attention and mixed domestic responses. Socially, migration pressures and human-rights questions under the exception regime drew domestic protest and international scrutiny, even as some segments supported Bukele’s security gains. Internationally, El Salvador sought new financial and diplomatic relationships, balancing ties with the United States while pursuing fintech and development initiatives.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Equatorial Guinea has remained under the long-standing presidency of Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, with the 2016 election extending his grip on power amid ongoing concerns about political competition and freedom of expression. The economy, historically driven by oil, faced a downturn in the early 2020s as commodity prices fell, intensifying policy focus on diversification, better governance, and human-capital investments to sustain development. Social indicators and rights continue to be a central issue, with international observers highlighting limited political space and uneven access to health and education despite oil wealth. Multilateral institutions have pressed for structural reforms to diversify revenue, strengthen macro-fiscal resilience, and improve public financial management, while Equatorial Guinea engages in international diplomacy and aid programs to bolster development and governance. In 2024–25, the country was involved in a territorial dispute with Gabon over nearby islands, and reports of security-linked interventions and internal investigations underscored ongoing concerns about governance and succession dynamics.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Eritrea and Ethiopia formally ended their two-decade state of war in July 2018, reopening ties, air and land links, and signaling potential regional economic opportunities; however, the long-running conflict left deep-seated mistrust and a complex security calculus that continued to influence policies in both countries. The Afwerki regime in Eritrea has maintained tight political control since independence, with limited civil liberties and a highly centralized economy, and it has been cautious about externally driven reform while resisting broad political openness. In the 2020s, Eritrea faced renewed regional pressures and shifting alliances, including cautious diplomacy with neighbors but ongoing tensions over security and border issues that complicated its international posture. Economically, growth remained constrained by state monopolies, international isolation, and dependence on a few sectors, even as some regional incentives and port access discussions offered potential strategic salience. By the mid-2020s, Eritrea’s international positioning was characterized by balancing a fragile regional security environment with selective engagement from external partners, even as sanctions and scrutiny persisted and the country faced ongoing human-rights and governance criticisms.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Estonia has deepened its Western alignment through ongoing NATO integration and sustained defense spending, including clear calls to maintain security commitments since the Warsaw Summit in 2016 and beyond. The country has continued to leverage its advanced digital governance and cyber capabilities, exemplified by sustained investments in national cyber resilience and the concept of a data embassy to protect government data during crises. Since 2016 Estonia’s domestic politics have seen stable pro-Western leadership, with several coalition reshuffles culminating in a 2022–2023 period under Prime Minister Kaja Kallas and a resilient Reform Party–led government; by 2024–2025 the political system remained institutionally stable even as security threats intensified. Estonia has actively shaped regional security diplomacy, chairing CBSS work and hosting NATO and European security dialogues, while expanding defense cooperation and ensuring public support for security and resilience measures. The economy, while not the sole focus, has benefited from diversified, innovation-led development and strong institutional capacity, reinforcing Estonia’s position as a model for e-government and secure digital infrastructure in Europe.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since taking office in 2018, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed launched a sweeping reform program aimed at opening politics, releasing detainees, and redefining Ethiopia's regional relations, including a historic peace with Eritrea. These reforms coincided with a dangerous security challenge, as the Tigray region descended into conflict in 2020, triggering a humanitarian crisis and disrupting governance. A breakthrough came in November 2022 when the government and the TPLF agreed to a permanent cessation of hostilities, mediated by the African Union, though other actors such as Eritrean forces remained outside the deal. From 2022 onward, there was a gradual return to negotiations and limited humanitarian access, with ongoing questions about political reforms and governance at the national level. Internationally, Ethiopia sought to reposition itself as a regional stabilizer and reformist partner, balancing relations with donors, the AU, and neighboring states while pursuing development projects and investment.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: The Falkland Islands Defence Force remains the island’s core local security unit, operating as a volunteer force that works alongside UK-supplied forces to safeguard the islands; in 2023 the fisheries protection vessel FPV Lilibet joined the fleet to police the surrounding EEZ. In the political sphere, elections in December 2025 produced a legislature elected by non-partisans, with no active political parties forming a government, reflecting long-standing local governance norms. International positioning continues to center on the UK’s sovereign claim and the islanders’ right to self-determination, while Argentina maintains its sovereignty claims and calls for dialogue, a stance that has persisted amid periodic diplomatic tension. Social and economic development have emphasized stability and housing demand planning, supported by recent national accounts and policy work through 2024, even as the economy shows modest growth and diversification efforts. Overall, security coordination with the UK remains a cornerstone of policy, even as the islands participate in regional and global discussions on sovereignty, defense, and governance.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Fiji’s political landscape has shifted from the Bainimarama-era governance to a more multilateral, reform-oriented state following the 2022 general election, which facilitated a peaceful transfer of power to the Fiji Labour Party–based coalition led by Sitiveni Rabuka. The security environment in recent years has emphasized climate-security linkages and regional partnerships, with Pacific regional security outlooks stressing the need for flexible mechanisms to address environmental disasters, cyber threats, and transnational crime. Social change has included ongoing governance reform debates and concerns about anti-corruption institutions, alongside efforts to address governance transparency and electoral integrity after decades of centralized rule. Economically, Fiji benefited from a rebound in tourism and investment in 2022–23, while institutions and development partners have urged continued structural reforms and prudent debt management to bolster resilience. Internationally, Fiji has positioned itself as a vocal advocate for climate action and regional unity within the Pacific, engaging actively in Pacific Islands Forum discussions and broader partnerships with major powers while seeking to preserve regional autonomy.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Finland’s security posture underwent a watershed shift when it formally joined NATO in 2023, reflecting a broader reorientation of its defense policy in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The domestic political scene stabilized around pragmatic coalition governance led by the 2023 parliamentary outcome and figures like Petteri Orpo, signaling a steady, results‑oriented approach rather than ideological upheaval. Internationally, Helsinki intensified cooperation within NATO, participated in large‑scale exercises such as Nordic Response 2024, and deepened defense collaboration with the United States as part of a broader realignment of Nordic security. Social and demographic policy remained a focal point, with ongoing debates over welfare, education, and integration as Finland adapts its social model to a changing population. Economically, Finland pursued resilience and innovation in areas like green technology and digital services, emphasizing sustainable development and social cohesion over headline growth figures.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: The French Southern and Antarctic Lands (TAAF) remain a sui generis French overseas collectivity with autonomous administration since 1955, housing no permanent residents but hosting scientific missions and military presence to assert sovereignty in the southern Indian Ocean and in Antarctica. In the past decade France has used regular patrols and resupply missions by the polar vessel L’Astrolabe to maintain authority over its exclusive economic zones and outlying island territories, including operations around the Éparses in the Mozambique Channel. Biodiversity and climate resilience have become central priorities, with new agreements and programs aimed at protecting marine ecosystems and coordinating science-based management under both national and interagency frameworks. France announced a major expansion of its natural marine protected area in the subantarctic region, reaching about 1.6 million square kilometers and reinforcing its role in global ocean conservation and biodiversity preservation. Amid these developments, TAAF’s international positioning emphasizes maritime domain leadership and a strengthened ecological stewardship model, aligning with broader French and EU interests in Antarctic science, fisheries governance, and regional cooperation in the southern oceans.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, France's political trajectory has centered on Emmanuel Macron's presidency and a cycle of reform attempts that sparked broad public debate. Security concerns remained prominent, with France deploying security forces to manage protests and facing ongoing counter-terrorism challenges. The Yellow Vests movement of 2018–2019 underscored social and regional inequalities and prompted Macron to launch a nationwide debate on civic grievances. Economically, the government pursued tax adjustments and pension reform while seeking to modernize France's economy within the EU, balancing growth with social pressure. France continued to project influence internationally through EU leadership, NATO alignment, and climate diplomacy, while engaging in Africa policy and development efforts.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Gabon’s political arc since 2016 has oscillated between entrenched dynastic rule and street- and military-led challenges, including a 2019 coup attempt and sustained protests after disputed elections that highlighted tensions over succession and accountability. In 2023 a military faction briefly toppled President Ali Bongo Ondimba, prompting international condemnations and long-running conversations about constitutional order and the army’s role in politics. A transitional authorities’ leadership, led by Brice Oligui Nguema, has since steered the country through a new phase of governance, with elections held and a shift toward institutional reform and a role for a civilian-led transition, though questions remain about era legitimacy and judicial accountability. The 2024–25 period saw formal moves to restructure the political system, including discussions around a new constitution and term limits, while Gabon’s international positioning has increasingly balanced relations with traditional partners in Africa, Europe, and the region, amid scrutiny of how resources and governance are managed.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: The Gambia’s political trajectory shifted dramatically after Adama Barrow’s 2016 presidential victory, ending Yahya Jammeh’s 22-year rule and ushering in a transition backed by ECOWAS that culminated in Barrow’s January 2017 oath and Jammeh’s exile. Barrow’s government pursued constitutional reforms, judicial strengthening, and preparations for a Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission to address past abuses, signaling a move away from the old regime’s authoritarian practices. Security and human rights conditions improved in the ensuing years as political prisoners were released and the security services underwent reform, with international attention and support focused on governance and accountability. The international profile of The Gambia rose as it rejoined the Commonwealth in 2018 and sought closer ties with donors and partners to address legacy economic challenges and foster inclusive development, aided by targeted aid and governance reforms. By the mid-2020s, The Gambia pursued a more stable, rights-respecting path while prioritizing social development and inclusive growth, aided by international institutions highlighting progress and continuing to monitor reforms.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Georgian Dream’s rise and victory in the 2012 parliamentary elections marked a durable shift in Georgia’s political landscape, followed by the 2016 elections being broadly orderly and later political clashes that underscored calls for reform. Russia’s ongoing occupations of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, along with Moscow’s broader regional influence, have remained the central security concern shaping Georgia’s strategic posture and defense planning. Domestic social mobilizations around governance, rule of law, and anti-corruption campaigns—including heated debates over foreign influence legislation and EU integration—have highlighted a highly polarized political climate and active civil society. The economy has seen diversification and investment in sectors like energy and infrastructure, but governance challenges and oligarchic influence have continued to constrain reform efforts and public trust. Georgia has pursued a Western-oriented trajectory with engagement with the EU and strategic partnerships with the United States and NATO allies, while balancing regional dynamics and security threats.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade Germany moved from Angela Merkel’s long‑standing centrist leadership to Olaf Scholz’s SPD‑Greens‑FDP coalition, marked by a shift in domestic politics and public appetite for reform; in security, Scholz declared a Zeitenwende after Russia’s 2022 invasion and pushed a major modernization push for the Bundeswehr while reaffirming NATO commitments; socially, Germany has continued grappling with migration, integration, and housing challenges alongside climate and energy policy debates; economically, it faced headwinds and a need to diversify energy sources and industrial strategy, balancing growth with resilience and structural reform; internationally, Berlin has pursued a more assertive European security posture, strengthened ties within NATO and the EU, and recalibrated energy and diplomatic relations in a changed global order.;

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2016, Ghana has seen a peaceful political transition to the New Patriotic Party (NPP) government under Nana Akufo-Addo, with subsequent elections consolidating a multi-party system and steady democratic norms. The early 2020s brought economic distress that culminated in an IMF-supported program starting in 2023, accompanied by reforms and expanded social protection aimed at protecting vulnerable households. The government also pursued targeted social interventions, such as cash-transfer programs, and debated widening access to education, framed within broader efforts to sustain inclusive development. Independent observers have highlighted Ghana’s resilient democracy, including high electoral democracy scores and steady civil liberties, even as the country navigated economic pressures and regional security challenges. Internationally, Ghana has rebuilt relations with creditors and leveraged IMF support to stabilize macroeconomic fundamentals while maintaining active regional diplomacy and trade links.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: From 2015 to 2019, Greece endured a deep austerity period under Syriza, culminating in a controversial bailout referendum and a subsequent reshaped policy path as creditors insisted on economic reforms. In 2019, New Democracy under Kyriakos Mitsotakis won, shifting to market-friendly reforms, privatizations, and a focus on digitalization to restart growth while maintaining fiscal discipline. Greece’s COVID-19 recovery strategy leaned on EU Recovery and Resilience Funds to support health, investment, and structural reforms, aiming to transform its economy toward green and digital transitions. Security and diplomacy fluctuated as tensions with Turkey flared intermittently, prompting renewed talks and high-level diplomacy within NATO and regional frameworks. Social and migration dynamics remained central, with refugee movements and domestic social cohesion shaping policy debates and resilience-building alongside continued reforms.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Greenland’s political landscape since self-rule deepened its path toward greater autonomy within the Kingdom of Denmark, with coalition governments emphasizing a more autonomous foreign, security, and defense posture framed by a 2024–2033 Arctic Strategy. The security environment in the Arctic has sharpened great-power competition and prompted Greenland to coordinate more closely with Denmark and allies while pursuing its own diplomatic space, including new Arctic and defense policy discussions. Socially, Greenland faces ongoing challenges rooted in colonial legacies and rapid modernization, shaping debates around health, social welfare, and national identity. Economically, Greenland seeks to diversify beyond fishing via mineral development under a 2020–2024 strategy, aiming to create jobs and long-term revenue while managing environmental and community concerns. Internationally, Greenland has maneuvered to broaden engagement—reopening the US consulate in 2020 and pursuing closer ties with a range of partners—while carefully balancing its relationship with Denmark and wider geopolitical dynamics in the Arctic.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Guatemala’s political trajectory since 2019 has been shaped by the transition from the CICIG-era crackdown on corruption to a more polarized governance environment under President Alejandro Giammattei and his successor, with ongoing concerns about judicial independence and prosecutions of political opponents; in security terms, the government has prioritized countering organized crime and extortion, even as violence remains a challenge and prisons have faced riots and security crackdowns. Socially, public protests and civil society campaigns against corruption have continued to influence national discourse, including contentious moves around the attorney general and constitutional court appointments. Economically, Guatemala has pursued development programs and resilience-building with support from international partners, notably the World Bank’s 2024–2027 Country Partnership Framework and road- and infrastructure-focused initiatives intended to connect remote regions and spur inclusive opportunities. Internationally, the country has sought to maintain close ties with the United States while integrating with regional and development actors, leveraging World Bank projects and IMF guidance to align public spending with development priorities.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since the 2021 coup, Guinea has been governed by a military transitional regime under Mamadi Doumbouya, with sustained international pressure from ECOWAS and the AU to return to civilian rule. The junta dissolved the government and restricted officials, drawing sanctions and diplomatic scrutiny from regional and global actors as it mapped a transitional path. By 2024–2025, promises to hold elections faced delays, even as regional mediators urged speed and some constitutional path toward civilian governance remained uncertain. The economy continued to depend on its vast bauxite resources, but social conditions and poverty persisted for many Guineans, complicating the political transition. Internationally, Guinea remained a focal point of West Africa diplomacy, with ECOWAS, the EU, and UN engagement shaping the trajectory toward a constitutional transfer of power.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Guinea-Bissau has endured repeated political upheavals since the mid-2010s, including protracted power struggles between presidents and parliaments that have tested constitutional norms. In 2020 Umaro Sissoco Embaló won the presidency and has faced ongoing tensions with rivals, periodic threats to dissolve parliament, and disputes over term limits that have drawn regional mediation from ECOWAS. The security landscape remained volatile through 2020–2023, with episodes of attempted coups and clashes involving presidential guards, prompting regional concerns about stability and civilian oversight of the armed forces. The government has pursued limited reforms and sought external support from international partners, while infrastructure and governance challenges have constrained service delivery and tax collection, fueling social and development concerns. In 2025–2026, international institutions and regional actors have continued to monitor elections and governance, highlighting persistent fragility but also ongoing engagement to stabilize institutions and promote orderly political competition.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Geopolitically, Guyana’s governing coalitions shifted in the last decade, with the APNU+AFC coalition losing power to the PPP/C in the 2020 general elections and the PPP/C under Irfaan Ali taking office, followed by Ali’s reaffirmation in 2025 for a second term.
