Security policy has prioritized intelligence-led policing and major investments in the Guyana Police Force, contributing to a substantial decline in serious crimes since 2020 and improving public safety metrics, even as domestic violence and rape remained concerns in some reports. Socially and economically, Guyana has pursued diversified development and social programs to manage the oil boom, while steering toward fiscal transparency and a sovereign wealth fund to govern oil revenues and avoid overheating the economy. Internationally, the oil windfall has reshaped foreign ties and development partnerships, with discussions around governance models and transparency as the country seeks to translate resource wealth into broader development.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2016 Haiti’s political trajectory has been punctured by repeated leadership crises and contested elections, culminating in the July 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moïse and a ruling-by-decree pattern under Prime Minister Ariel Henry that faced limited parliamentary legitimacy. The security landscape deteriorved sharply in 2023–24 as gangs expanded control over broad areas of Port‑au‑Prince, led to mass displacements, prison breaks, and attacks on critical infrastructure, prompting international discussions of a multinational stabilization presence. International partners intensified engagement on governance, anti‑corruption, and humanitarian relief, with the IMF and World Bank stressing governance reforms, while Kenya agreed to lead a UN‑backed security mission to support stabilization efforts. In parallel, Haiti’s economy and social fabric faced shocks from natural disasters, inflation, and food insecurity, underscoring the urgency of restoration of basic services and resilient institutions, even as local civil society and Haitian institutions pressed for credible transitions and elections. By 2024–25, a transitional political framework and international security support began reshaping expectations for a path toward credible elections, though real improvements in daily security and rule of law remained uneven and closely tied to ongoing displacement and humanitarian needs.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Honduras’s political landscape since 2013 has been dominated by the National Party and then by shifting dynamics around controversial reelection and later governance under Xiomara Castro’s LIBRE administration, reshaping electoral and institutional debates. The country’s security policy moved from hardline gang suppression toward international cooperation and reform efforts, including U.S. support for coordinated policing and judicial reforms, while facing persistent violence and crime concerns. Social and migratory trends remained pronounced, with emigration continuing to be a central livelihood strategy for many families amid limited economic opportunity and public concerns about governance. The economy has seen uneven development and poverty reduction efforts alongside political controversy over investment models and special zones, including ZEDEs and related disputes that captivated domestic and international attention. Honduras has increasingly positioned itself within regional and international fora, balancing traditional partners with new governance challenges and scrutiny over rule of law, corruption, and civil liberties under a state of exception introduced in late 2022.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2010, Hungary under Viktor Orbán and the Fidesz party has centralized political power, reshaped institutions, and tightened control over media and civil society, creating a more centralized governing framework by the end of the 2010s. The European Union began in 2023–2024 to push back on Hungary’s rule-of-law reforms and related sovereignty measures, opening infringement procedures and conditioning access to cohesion funds for how Budapest enforces national rules. Hungary has maintained a distinctive stance on the Ukraine war, remaining a NATO member and reluctant to arm Kyiv while preserving closer ties with Moscow, a posture that has helped keep it at odds with some EU colleagues. Energy policy has intensified international scrutiny around the Paks nuclear expansion with Rosatom, a project framed by Budapest as essential for security and affordability but contested by critics over dependence on Russia. Domestically, Budapest has continued to defend its policy mix through public consultations and legal reforms that its government argues protect sovereignty but which EU partners see as eroding democratic norms and complicating bloc-level funding and policy alignment.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: The 2016 Panama Papers–triggered protests helped precipitate early elections and a shift to coalition governance, reshaping Iceland’s political landscape and reinforcing demands for reform and greater transparency. Iceland has maintained an active role in transatlantic security through NATO, with high-level engagement and ongoing OSCE and Nordic security discussions shaping its security policy into the mid‑2020s. The government has also emphasized gender balance and youth representation, notably with Gudlaugur Þór Þórðarson’s foreign ministry tenure and Iceland’s relatively younger leadership in its diplomatic corps. Economically, Iceland has pursued stabilizing macro policies, a green transition, and financial resilience following the pandemic, with IMF and OECD assessments highlighting disciplined policy and gradual debt reduction alongside structural reforms. Internationally, Iceland continues its EU‑related work and Arctic diplomacy, balancing EU cooperation, bilateral trade adaptations, and enhanced participation in multilateral programs while leveraging its Arctic and transatlantic links.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Narendra Modi’s BJP government won a decisive 2014 mandate and set a trajectory focused on economic reforms, a strong nationalist narrative, and expanded international engagement. The ensuing years saw major policy shifts including the 2016 demonetization and the 2017 Goods and Services Tax reform, aimed at formalizing the economy and boosting investment, though they also caused short-term disruption and drew mixed employment outcomes. In the 2019 elections, Modi secured a second term with a broader foreign policy footprint, reinforcing ties with the United States and other partners while navigating regional security challenges and arms-market opportunities. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed vulnerabilities in health, supply chains, and jobs, prompting policy responses toward digital governance, resilience, and inclusive growth, even as long-term job creation remained a pressing concern. Since 2020, India has sought a more assertive international role—balancing Western partnerships with engagement in multilateral forums and regional coalitions—while pursuing a diversified economy agenda that emphasizes digital services, manufacturing with domestic reforms, and climate and infrastructure investments.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since Jokowi took office in 2014, Indonesia pursued large-scale infrastructure and social programs while grappling with entrenched graft and regulatory challenges, shaping a decade of reform and pushback that left mixed perceptions of political change. The country maintained a steady security posture, mounting maritime enforcement against illegal fishing and counterterrorism efforts as part of a broader national security agenda. The 2024 presidential election culminated in Prabowo Subianto’s victory and a transition to a new administration, marking a return to a more traditional power structure after Jokowi’s tenure. Internationally, Indonesia expanded its diplomacy within ASEAN and the G20, while seeking to balance relations with major powers on climate, trade, and regional security. Social and technological change helped drive urban growth and digitalization, even as protests and debates over democracy and governance kept public discourse vibrant.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since the JCPOA was agreed in 2015 and implemented in 2016, Iran pursued a path of limited engagement with the West on its nuclear program under a reform-minded leadership, but the U.S. withdrawal from the deal in 2018 and subsequent sanctions significantly curtailed Tehran’s diplomacy and economy; with President Ebrahim Raisi taking office in 2021, the political trajectory shifted toward a more conservative, security-focused stance, emphasizing internal stability and a strengthened security apparatus. The 2022–2023 Woman, Life, Freedom protests highlighted sustained social resilience, especially among younger Iranians, and triggered a harsh government crackdown alongside renewed international attention to rights concerns and political legitimacy. Iran’s economy has faced persistent strains from sanctions, inflation, and external disruptions, with the World Bank noting contraction pressures and uncertainty about the outlook as a key constraint on domestic demand and investment. International positioning has involved attempts to balance partners and leverage regional influence, maintaining a degree of strategic autonomy while navigating continued pressure over sanctions and security issues, as reflected in ongoing discussions around reviving or adjusting the JCPOA and Iran’s broader foreign policy conduct.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2016, Iraq has pushed to consolidate security after the territorial defeat of ISIS, but persistent militia influence and sporadic violence have continued to complicate governance and security planning. The 2021 parliamentary elections triggered a lengthy political crisis that culminated in a new government under Mohammed Shia al-Sudani in October 2022, signaling a shift toward a cabinet with stronger Iranian-backed influence in practice. Tensions over oil revenues and exports with the Kurdistan Region persisted, including disputes over Kurdish oil sales and the 2023 budget framework that aimed to curb Erbil’s autonomy, with partial resumption of Kurdish exports occurring in 2023–2024. The economy remained constrained by oil dependence, budget frictions, and inflation, while reconstruction and diversification progressed sluggishly amid governance fragility and competing pressures. International positioning saw Iraq balancing US and Iranian influence as the coalition presence waned, with Baghdad seeking greater sovereign control over security while pursuing bilateral security arrangements and regional diplomacy.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since the 2016 general election, Fine Gael led a minority government that gradually moved Irish politics beyond historic Civil War-era rivalries, culminating in a 2020 confidence-and-supply agreement and then a three‑party coalition with Fianna Fáil and the Green Party. In 2018 Ireland held a landmark referendum to repeal the Eighth Amendment and subsequently enacted the Health (Regulation of Termination of Pregnancy) Act 2018, marking a rapid social liberalization on abortion. The COVID‑19 pandemic dominated public policy from 2020 into 2021, with the government publishing resilience and recovery plans and implementing phased measures to protect lives while supporting the economy. The 2020s also saw internal coalition tensions and policy contestation around budgets, housing, climate action, and social reform, though the government remained in power and continued to govern through changing electoral dynamics. Ireland has sought to preserve a stable EU-oriented international stance, balancing domestic reforms with its role in European and global economic governance, including ongoing engagement in fiscal and regulatory reforms tied to global tax initiatives.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Israel’s last decade has been defined by a major security confrontation following Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack, which precipitated a Gaza war and widespread international scrutiny of legal and humanitarian issues. The domestic political scene experienced sustained controversy over judicial reform and governance, contributing to social protests and realignments within the coalition and opposition alike. Economically, Israel maintained resilience through technology-led growth and international financing while enduring prolonged conflict, with analysts noting normalization of markets and continued investment activity despite instability. Internationally, Israel faced high-profile legal actions and diplomacy around the Gaza war, including ICC warrants and sustained engagement with Western allies and regional partners amid shifting regional dynamics. The humanitarian and human-rights dimensions of the Gaza crisis, alongside ongoing violence in the West Bank, continued to shape Israel’s global positioning and its relations with the United Nations, European Union, and other key partners.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Italy’s political landscape shifted dramatically from 2018 onward as a populist coalition between the Five Star Movement and the League then collapsed in 2019, leading to new arrangements and reforms under successive administrations, including the technocratic Draghi government that steered Italy through the pandemic and European Union recovery funds. The country’s security and migration policies intensified debates at home and with the EU, while Italy’s role in EU policy—especially regarding asylum rules, fiscal support, and coordination on Ukraine—moved toward greater alignment with Brussels during the Draghi era and beyond. Economically, Italy weathered COVID-19 with a strong rebound aided by Next Generation EU resources, though high debt and uneven growth remained long‑standing challenges even as exports and services recovered. Social change continued to be shaped by demographic pressures and populist discourse, with 2022 marking a new phase as right‑of‑center leadership under Giorgia Meloni reshaped Italy’s international positioning and domestic policy trajectory. Italy’s international posture increasingly emphasized prudent fiscal stewardship, EU integration, and strategic diplomacy in Europe and beyond, balancing domestic political shifts with commitments to energy resilience and regional stability.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since winning the 2016 general election, the Jamaica Labour Party under Prime Minister Andrew Holness has pursued fiscal discipline and IMF program compliance, reinforcing investor confidence and yielding credit-rating improvements. Security has seen a notable, though uneven, improvement with official reports of gang alignment and murder rates easing in the early 2020s, alongside continued policing investments and modernization. Jamaica also advanced social reform by decriminalizing marijuana in 2015 and moving toward a regulatory framework for medical cannabis, with ongoing debates about economic and social impacts. The economy has benefited from a buoyant tourism sector and resilience measures following the COVID-19 shock, underpinned by macroeconomic policies tied to the IMF program and debt-management efforts. International positioning has included deeper engagement with CARICOM and regional partners, emphasizing debt sustainability, climate resilience, and Jamaica’s role as a relatively stable hub in the Caribbean, even as fiscal and security challenges persist.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2016, Japan’s security policy has shifted from a postwar pacifist norm toward a more proactive defense posture, driven by constitutional reinterpretation and new security legislation enacted around 2015–2016. In 2022, Tokyo unveiled a revamped National Security Strategy and National Defense Strategy, signaling higher deterrence thresholds and closer alliance coordination with the United States and partners in the Indo-Pacific. The Kishida and Suga administrations pursued economic and social policy agendas while grappling with a rapidly aging society, aiming to stabilize public finances and sustain growth in a difficult macro environment. Japan has actively sought a more assertive regional foothold through participation in regional forums and steps toward shaping a broader Indo-Pacific order. Demographic decline and aging continue to frame policy across health care, immigration, and labor as well as the strategic calculations driving security and economic planning.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, Jordan steered macro stability under IMF programs, culminating in a four-year Extended Fund Facility approved in January 2024 to support reform and resilience. The kingdom continued gradual political reform and parliamentary engagement while balancing security challenges at its borders and amid regional upheaval. Domestic social pressures and refugee hosting remained central to policy debates, shaping budgets and calls for targeted employment and development programs. Jordan pressurized by external shocks and debt dynamics pursued structural reforms to improve competitiveness, energy pricing, and public finances without relying on growth headlines. Regionally, Amman maintained its balanced diplomacy with the United States and neighboring states, striving to preserve stability and secure aid and investment.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: From 2019 Kassym-Jomart Tokayev took office, signaling a gradual shift away from Nazarbayev’s personalist legacy while promising political reform. The January 2022 protests escalated into nationwide unrest and led to a CSTO intervention and a purge of Nazarbayev-era networks, highlighting elite realignments and security concerns. In June 2022 a constitutional referendum reduced Nazarbayev’s formal powers and reshaped political institutions, reinforcing Tokayev’s consolidation of control. The government has pursued economic diversification and modernization in the context of Russia’s war in Ukraine, attempting to balance Moscow and Beijing while preserving Kazakhstan’s regional role. Kazakhstan has also sought a more active international footprint, including non-permanent membership on the UN Security Council and broader regional diplomacy.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: In the last decade Kenya has navigated a turbulent but stabilizing political path, including a contested 2017 election that led to a Supreme Court-ordered rerun and broader governance reforms within the Jubilee era. The 2018 “handshake” between Uhuru Kenyatta and Raila Odinga helped ease street tensions and reshaped alliance politics, even as rivalries resurfaced ahead of the 2022 vote. Security remained a central concern, with sustained Kenyan military involvement in Somalia against al-Shabaab and persistent cross-border threats that shaped regional counterterrorism cooperation. Economically, Kenya continued diversifying beyond traditional sectors toward technology, finance, and infrastructure, while many households faced cost-of-living pressures and uneven development across counties. Internationally, Kenya positioned itself as a regional hub for East Africa through active diplomacy, regional security efforts, and engagement with global partners, even as questions about governance, corruption, and social inclusion persisted.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Kosovo has pursued European integration while navigating a notably fragile political landscape, including a 2025 parliamentary election that was welcomed as peaceful and saw increased women’s representation. The Kosovo Security Force’s evolving mandate and continued NATO support, alongside ongoing Belgrade–Pristina dialogue, have kept security concerns central to politics and regional stability. Energy diversification and reform have become a priority, with Kosovo adopting a National Energy Strategy and pursuing reforms to expand generation capacity and improve efficiency. Macroeconomic stability has remained a work in progress, with IMF and World Bank assessments highlighting the need for reform, fiscal buffers, and a more conducive environment for investment amid political stalemate. International positioning remains crucial, as Kosovo operates under a Stabilization and Association Agreement with the EU and seeks closer Western integration while its status as a potential EU candidate keeps external support and conditionality at the forefront of policy discussions.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Kuwait experienced sustained parliamentary–government gridlock through much of the 2020s, with frequent cabinet resignations and the assembly clashing over spending, reforms and oversight, a pattern that reflected enduring tensions between elected lawmakers and the ruling establishment. The 2022 snap elections were followed by a Constitutional Court ruling in March 2023 that annulled that vote and reinstated the 2020 parliament, signaling a high-stakes legal and political contest over legitimacy and processes. In early 2023 and again in 2024, the emir dissolved parliament amid ongoing disputes, underscoring the firmness of the ruling family's control even as opposition figures reentered politics and new electoral rounds were pursued. Economically, Kuwait has pushed a diversification agenda under development plans such as New Kuwait 2035 and the Kuwait National Development Plan 2020–25, aimed at expanding non-oil sectors and improving the investment climate to insulate the economy from oil-price volatility. Internationally, Kuwait has sought to balance its long-standing alliance with the United States with regional diplomacy and investment, while positioning itself as a stabilizing actor in the Gulf amid broader shifts in energy, security and governance in the region.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Kyrgyzstan’s political trajectory over the past decade has been defined by periodic leadership turnover and a shift toward stronger executive influence following the 2020 protests and the 2021 constitutional changes. Security policy has prioritized counterterrorism and border management, with sustained attention to maintaining stability amid regional pressures and periodic security concerns raised by protests and organized crime networks. Social changes have included ongoing protests over governance and freedom of speech, alongside reform efforts aimed at expanding social services and addressing regional disparities, though public trust remains volatile. The economy has faced vulnerabilities tied to remittances, energy projects, and investment climate, while reform programs and development financing from international partners have sought to modernize infrastructure, governance, and the business environment without overemphasizing growth rates. International positioning has seen Kyrgyzstan navigate relations with Russia, China, and regional bodies like the SCO and CSTO, leveraging security cooperation and economic ties to preserve sovereignty and regional influence amid a fluid Central Asian landscape.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2016 Laos has maintained single‑party rule under the Lao People’s Revolutionary Party, prioritizing political stability and continuity within elite circles while resisting significant pluralism. The security environment has grown more Chinese‑leaning, with a rising security footprint in the region and cautious balancing by Laos amid broader US–China rivalries. Social change has brought higher education and urbanization, but civil space remains tightly constrained and recent protests have tested the regime’s grip on legitimacy. The economy remains exposed to external shocks and debt pressures even as infrastructure projects, including rail and energy networks tied to China’s Belt and Road push, drive development debates and debt risks. International positioning has leaned toward China and regional integration efforts, with government aims to graduate from least‑developed status by 2030 contributing to a pragmatic, status‑quo foreign policy.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade Latvia has reinforced its security posture through NATO integration and Baltic defense cooperation, building on long-standing commitments and participating in enhanced forward presence with steady political support for stronger deterrence. The 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine sharpened regional unity and accelerated defense spending, with Latvia signaling continued high levels of military investment and active participation in NATO and allied missions. Politically, Latvia has pursued pro-EU and pro-NATO stances while navigating domestic debates on governance, social inclusion, and energy independence amid European green and digital transitions. The country has leveraged EU funds and the Recovery and Resilience Facility to modernize infrastructure, housing, healthcare, and energy efficiency, aiming to boost resilience without focusing solely on growth rates. Internationally, Latvia has sought to position itself as a credible regional partner and ally, strengthening ties with the United States and EU partners while promoting security cooperation in the Baltic region and Ukraine-related reform efforts.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: From 2019 Lebanon saw unprecedented street protests that erupted over tax hikes, corruption, and governance, signaling broad demand for change beyond sectarian blocs. The August 2020 Beirut port explosion intensified public anger and worsened an already dire economic crisis, contributing to a deep political stalemate and loss of faith in institutions. By 2021 the country entered a severe financial collapse with currency depreciation, widespread poverty, and ongoing power shortages, prompting discussions of reform and international support like the Reform, Recovery, and Reconstruction Framework (3RF). A new government under Najib Mikati formed in 2021 after extended deadlock, but persistent political fragmentation and external influence from regional actors continued to shape Lebanon’s policy choices and its prospects for stabilization. Across society, social distress grew alongside diaspora remittances, while international positioning remained cautious as donors and creditors linked aid to governance and reform, even as electricity, public services, and livelihoods remained fragile.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2012 Lesotho has experienced repeated coalition governments and notable political volatility, with two coalitions collapsing and a pattern of shifting party alliances shaping governance in quick succession. The security environment has been punctuated by intermittent unrest and a high-profile 2014 attempted coup involving the Lesotho Defence Force, followed by ongoing legal and institutional follow-up surrounding the episode. Social policy has focused on extending development planning through measures like the extended NSDP II, alongside governance reforms and social contracts aimed at improving public service delivery and accountability. Economically, the kingdom continues to rely on SACU revenues and a private-sector push toward export-led growth, with policy emphasis on diversification and private investment under NSDP II extensions into 2027/28. Internationally, Lesotho has sought stronger regional security and development partnerships through SADC and cooperation with multilateral donors, positioning itself as a collaborative participant in southern Africa’s stability and growth agenda.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2018 Liberia’s leadership transition to George Weah marked the country’s first peaceful power handover in decades, signaling a new era of political legitimacy and executive accountability amid persistent governance and security challenges. The Weah era confronted the aftermath of the Ebola outbreak and global shocks, with policy emphasis on anti-corruption measures, business climate improvements, and rebuilding public services. By 2021–2022 Liberia began a cautious macroeconomic rebound, aided by prudent fiscal policy and a focus on diversified mining, agriculture, and infrastructure, while poverty and service delivery remained stubbornly salient. In 2024 Joseph Boakai won the presidency, promising renewed transparency and public‑sector reforms, and Liberia’s international engagement intensified as it sought to broaden regional and global partnerships. Overall, Liberia has sought to stabilize its security situation, strengthen institutions, and pursue development with continued international support and governance reforms.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Libya’s political landscape has remained deeply divided since 2014, with rival authorities—the eastern-based House of Representatives and the Libyan National Army and the western UN-backed Government of National Accord—contending for legitimacy, resources, and influence, a division long described in UN and academic analyses and solidified by the 2015 Libyan Political Agreement establishing the GNA. Haftar’s 2019–2020 offensive aimed at seizing Tripoli highlighted the security dimension of the crisis, drawing backing from Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, and Russia on one side and Turkish support for the GNA on the other, before a 2020 cease-fire began to stabilize fighting zones. In 2021 Libya finally tested a path toward unity with the formation of a Government of National Unity, the first attempt at a single national government in years, though the arrangement faced persistent resistance and an unsettled political roadmap in subsequent years. By 2023–2024, Libya’s political impasse persisted even as the UN and regional actors pressed for a Libyan-led settlement, while social and economic strains continued to shape migration, security, and governance challenges across the country. Internationally, oil resources and foreign sponsorships continued to drive Libya’s external alignments, with shifting leverage over ports and revenues influencing bargaining among factions and neighbors.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Lithuania’s political system consolidated after 2016 with a stable democratic trajectory culminating in President Gitanas Nausėda’s 2019 election and a cautious reform agenda in government through 2024. NATO and EU security priorities shaped policy, with Lithuania hosting and welcoming enhanced forward presence and the arrival of German troops in 2022 to deter threats on the eastern flank. Energy and economic diversification progressed through measures like the Klaipėda LNG terminal expansion and regional regasification capacity arrangements to reduce dependence on single suppliers. The outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022 intensified security concerns, led Lithuania to declare a state of emergency, and spurred stronger NATO deployments and unity among Baltic states. Domestic debates over governance and anti-corruption reform continued to influence policy from 2020 to 2024, even as the government sought to address public sector integrity and procurement practices.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Luxembourg has tracked a relatively stable, centrist political path over the last decade, beginning in 2013 with a coalition led by Prime Minister Xavier Bettel of the DP that linked the DP, LSAP and Greens, and continuing through Bettel's govern­ments after 2018, despite evolving party dynamics; Bettel’s coalition was challenged by results in the October 2023 election, which reduced its parliamentary majority and prompted a shift in the ruling arrangement, though Bettel remained a key figure in government until a new coalition formed; the country has also sought to strengthen its international profile within the EU and beyond, leveraging its small-state diplomacy and permanent roles in European institutions; economically, Luxembourg has faced external demand-driven weakness and a 2023 contraction even as the financial sector remained a central engine and showed resilience in 2024, with ongoing diversification and prudential safeguards highlighted by the IMF; socially, Luxembourg has pursued inclusive policy steps such as the 2020 introduction of free public transport, reflecting a broader social model that intertwines mobility, welfare and urban development; ([gouvernement.lu](https://gouvernement.lu/en/gouvernement/xavier-bettel/biographie.html?utm_source=openai))

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: After a long, decades-long dispute with Greece, North Macedonia courted a turning point in 2018 by agreeing to a new name under the Prespa Agreement, a move that unlocked NATO accession and opened the door to European Union talks. In March 2020, the country joined NATO, marking a major security milestone after years of vetoes and diplomatic wrangling. The EU path was revived but remained entangled in broader Western Balkans enlargement dynamics and internal reform requirements, with formal negotiations anticipated but uneven across time. Domestically, successive governments pursued constitutional and legal reforms tied to EU and NATO integration, including language and minority-law considerations that featured prominently in reform agendas. Internationally, North Macedonia positioned itself as a stabilizing partner in the region, balancing relations with EU and NATO allies while managing neighborly disputes and ongoing social-change debates.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since the 2018 presidential election, Madagascar has moved toward greater political stability under President Andry Rajoelina, although governance challenges and periodic cabinet reshuffles remain a feature of its recent politics. The security environment has historically been fragile, with past coups and military influence; by the mid-2020s the authorities were more focused on maintaining order while avoiding renewed political crises. Socially, the government has pursued reforms to improve basic services and governance, backed by international partners, even as deep development needs and inequality persist. Economically, the country weathered the COVID-19 shock and a 2020–2021 downturn, with signs of recovery around 2024 but a continued need for structural reforms to boost inclusivity and growth quality. Internationally, Madagascar has engaged with the World Bank, IMF and regional partners to stabilize macroeconomics, attract investment, and align with SADC and other development programs while navigating aid flows and external shocks.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Malawi’s political landscape shifted decisively in 2020 when the Constitutional Court annulled the May 2019 presidential election, leading to a rerun in which Lazarus Chakwera defeated incumbent Peter Mutharika and was sworn in on June 28, 2020, marking a historic transfer of power through a court-ordered vote reversal. The Chakwera administration pursued anti-corruption and governance reforms while navigating a challenging economic environment marked by rising living costs and debt pressures, aided at times by international financial institutions and donor programs. Security and governance challenges persisted, including accountability efforts by bodies like the Human Rights Commission and ongoing scrutiny of election administration and judiciary independence, all set against Malawi’s fragile rural economy and climate-related shocks. International positioning shifted toward donor engagement and regional cooperation, with emphasis on governance, transparency, and development assistance as essential levers for stability and growth. By 2024–2025, Malawi’s electoral drama continued to influence political rhetoric and policy priorities, as authorities balanced reform agendas with public demands for relief from economic hardship and improved social services, amid a landscape of evolving party dynamics and leadership changes.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: The 2018 general election ended Barisan Nasional's long rule as Pakatan Harapan defeated BN and Mahathir Mohamad became prime minister, signaling a potential democratic renewal. The PH government pursued anti-corruption reforms but collapsed in February 2020 after defections in what became known as the Sheraton Move, triggering a swift political realignment. A new Perikatan Nasional coalition under Muhyiddin Yassin then took power, entering a period of persistent political turbulence and parliamentary maneuvering. By 2022-2023, Malaysia experienced a hung parliament, followed by the formation of a Unity Government led by Anwar Ibrahim in a coalition that included PH and BN, aiming to stabilize governance and push reforms. Economically, Malaysia navigated the COVID-19 shock, pursued diversification and infrastructure development, and maintained active regional and international engagement, balancing ties with major powers and regional partners.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade Mali has moved from a volatile political transition after dual coups in 2020 and 2021 to a military-led government entrenched in power, with evolving governance arrangements and limited progress on a civilian-led transition. Security has deteriorated as international peacekeeping missions ended and jihadist and inter-communal violence persisted, culminating in MINUSMA’s withdrawal in 2023 and a broader shift toward Malian-led counterinsurgency with foreign mercenaries at times implicated in abuses. Socially, the country faced displacement, school closures, and fuel blockades that disrupted ordinary life and exposed the vulnerability of civilians to ongoing violence and economic shocks. Economically, Mali weathered shocks since 2020 but remained challenged by inflation and external pressures while seeking new international alignments and development partnerships amid growing diplomatic isolation, including shifts in French and UN involvements and the emergence of other regional actors.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Mauritania’s political scene over the past decade has featured a continued, though imperfect, move toward civilian governance punctuated by lingering military influence, a landmark but cautious peaceful transfer of power in 2019, and growing concern about democratic backsliding and civil liberties. The security landscape has been shaped by regional Sahel instability and domestic counterterrorism efforts, with the state juggling security priorities against human rights criticisms and the need to protect vulnerable communities. Social change saw progress like the 2015 anti-slavery law and subsequent activism, but enforcement remains inconsistent and rights groups warn of implementation gaps. The economy has remained vulnerable to global commodity swings, even as development planning—such as the SCAPP strategy (2016–2030) and investments in energy and mining—seeks diversification and broader growth. International positioning has involved balancing development aid with concerns about governance and human rights while engaging partners across Africa, the Gulf, and global institutions amid calls for transparent governance and social inclusion.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: From taking office on December 1, 2018, AMLO’s administration framed its governance around a “Fourth Transformation” aimed at reducing inequality, expanding social programs, and pursuing anti-corruption reforms. The security policy shifted toward civilian-led approaches, with the creation of the National Guard and a management style summarized as “abrazos no balazos,” though critics and observers note ongoing violence and institutional tensions. By 2024, the administration faced persistent security challenges, judicial pushback, and crowding reform debates despite some social gains and policy changes. Economically, the government emphasized transfers to the poor, wage increases, and labor reform, while observers cautioned that poverty reduction did not automatically translate into broad-based development and that growth strategies remained contested. International positioning leaned on US-MMexico ties and regional diplomacy, all while domestic governance debates over the judiciary and security policy influenced Mexico’s credibility abroad.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since Maia Sandu’s 2020 election Moldova has pursued pro‑European reforms, prioritizing anti‑corruption efforts and judiciary overhaul after a constitutional crisis earlier that year, while navigating intense domestic and external pressures. The 2021 parliamentary vote gave Sandu‑led PAS full control, enabling a more coherent reform agenda though oligarchic influence and political fragility remained challenges. The 2022 war in Ukraine tested Moldova’s security and energy resilience, prompting cybersecurity legislation and a careful balancing of support for Ukraine with relations with Russia. Domestic politics continued to be affected by pro‑Western alignment and Kremlin‑linked interference, including 2023 court rulings and bans on pro‑Russian parties amid electoral tensions. From 2023 into 2024, the government under Dorin Recean pushed security, justice reform, and EU accession talks, maintaining a trajectory toward European integration amid regional pressures.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Mongolia’s political system underwent a notable consolidation after constitutional reforms in 2019 that strengthened the prime minister’s role and redefined presidential terms, contributing to greater executive stability through the early 2020s. The country has balanced security concerns and regional diplomacy while expanding engagement with international institutions, including a focus on responsible mining governance and ESG considerations. Its economy remains heavily mining-dependent, with policy emphasis on diversification and resilience amid global price volatility and geopolitical tensions, accompanied by continued fiscal prudence and investment in domestic demand. Social and educational reform efforts have sought to broaden skills and employment opportunities to reduce vulnerability to commodity cycles. Mongolia’s international positioning has increasingly framed itself as a climate-conscious, resource-based economy seeking stable partnerships and diversified export routes, even as the mining sector remains the main driver of macro performance.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Montenegro joined NATO in 2017 after the 2016 signing of its Accession Protocol, cementing its security alignment with Western institutions. The domestic political landscape over the past decade has been characterized by a long-dominant governing party and ongoing EU accession negotiations, with reform efforts under a revised enlargement framework beginning around 2021. On security and governance, Montenegro has faced AML/CFT and corruption challenges tied to financial flows and real estate, prompting calls for strengthened regulatory safeguards and anti-money‑laundering measures. The economy has benefited from a tourism-led rebound and consumption growth, while public debt remains a persistent constraint and IMF‑backed reforms aim to improve investment planning and resilience. Internationally, Montenegro maintains active roles in security and regional stability as a NATO member and EU candidate, with EU accession talks advancing through multiple chapters and continued Western Balkan integration efforts as of 2026.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since Morocco's 2011 constitutional reforms, the elected government gained greater parliamentary heft while the king retained decisive executive authority. The decade saw continued security concerns tied to Western Sahara, culminating in the 2020 U.S. recognition of Moroccan sovereignty and ensuing international debate and domestic crackdowns. Socially, Morocco experienced persistent mobilization and reforms under King Mohammed VI, with activists pushing for more rights and institutions, though critics say reforms were cautious. Economically, the country pursued diversification and development plans, including investment in industry and energy, while maintaining stability and attracting foreign investment. Internationally, Rabat shifted its posture by normalizing ties with Israel in 2020 and navigating European and regional diplomacy, with France later signaling support for its Western Sahara position.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2017 Mozambique has faced a severe Islamist insurgency in Cabo Delgado that disrupted security and development efforts, drawing in regional partners and international forces to stabilize the area. The Southern African Development Community and Rwanda-led forces substantially expanded security operations, while the central government grappled with governance challenges and human rights concerns amid ongoing conflict. In 2024, contested presidential election results triggered protests and a crackdown that intensified civilian harm and displacement, highlighting limits on political space and the fragility of public institutions. By 2025–2026, attention shifted to rebuilding and diversification, with heavy international involvement in energy development and security arrangements as projects like TotalEnergies’ gas venture sought restart amid volatility. The humanitarian toll remained acute, with large-scale displacements, food insecurity, and climate-related shocks shaping the social and economic landscape alongside Mozambique’s international positioning as a security and development partner in the region.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Myanmar’s 2015 elections brought the long-ruling military-backed system to a nominally civilian government under Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy, marking the country’s first widely contested vote in decades and a shift toward limited reform and greater international engagement. From 2016 into 2019, the reform era saw some easing of political restrictions, partial ceasefire efforts with ethnic armed groups, and a degree of social and administrative experimentation, even as the military retained substantial constitutional power and security prerogatives. On February 1, 2021, the military seized power in a coup, detaining Suu Kyi and other officials and triggering nationwide protests, a brutal crackdown, and a deep political and humanitarian crisis that provoked widespread international condemnation and targeted sanctions. Since then, Myanmar has experienced sustained resistance from civil society and ethnic groups, with the army facing ongoing internal conflict and a fragmented political landscape complicating governance and development. ASEAN-led diplomacy and Western sanctions have continued to shape Myanmar’s international positioning, while humanitarian needs and displacement have remained persistent concerns for neighboring states and global aid agencies.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since his 2020 election, TRNC President Ersin Tatar has advocated a two-state solution, signaling a shift from federation talks and aligning more closely with Ankara. Ankara-backed diplomacy and limited international recognition continue to constrain the TRNC's formal standing, with Turkey's support shaping security and the economy. The island's eastern Mediterranean energy discoveries and Turkish drilling near Cypriot waters have raised EU tensions and complicated prospects for reunification. Domestic politics in the north have faced criticism over governance and potential legal scrutiny of property commissions, amid social strains and calls for elections. Internationally, the TRNC remains unrecognized apart from Turkey, with EU and UN bodies pressing for sovereignty respect and negotiations on Cyprus’s future.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Namibia’s political arc over the past decade has seen long-time SWAPO leadership tested by changing voter expectations, culminating in the death of President Hage Geingob in February 2024 and a swift transitional arrangement. In November 2024, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah was elected president, becoming Namibia’s first female head of state, while SWAPO retained a narrow parliamentary majority amid logistical concerns that marred the vote. The IMF and other observers highlighted structural economy constraints, notably a reliance on mining and public wages, while stressing the need for diversification and private-sector job creation to sustain growth. Namibia has continued to position itself as a regional stability-maker and reform advocate, deepening ties with partners and seeking to mobilize development finance for energy, infrastructure, and social protection programs. Public frustration with governance and delivery has been foregrounded in policy debates, even as the country maintained its role in regional diplomacy and climate adaptation efforts.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Nepal promulgated a new constitution in 2015, completing a transition to federal parliamentary governance after years of civil conflict and political deadlock, though disputes over provincial boundaries and inclusion persisted in subsequent years. Security pressures eased after the end of the Maoist insurgency, but the country faced recurring political instability, including a near constitutional crisis in 2021 as parties realigned around changing coalitions. The post-2015 era saw reconstruction following the devastating 2015 earthquake, with reconstruction governance and disaster preparedness remaining central to development debates and local governance gradually gaining traction, aided by international partners and reconstruction authorities. Economically, Nepal diversified beyond traditional sectors, emphasizing infrastructure and development projects while relief and reconstruction needs highlighted governance gaps and the importance of social inclusion, literacy, and rural development. Internationally, Nepal sought to balance its relationships with neighboring powers and multilateral partners, leveraging humanitarian aid and development assistance to advance its security, governance, and development priorities, even as domestic challenges shaped its positioning on the regional stage.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: From 2010 to 2024, Mark Rutte led a series of coalitions in the Netherlands, but by 2025 the cabinet collapsed amid disputes over migration and far-right pressures, prompting a reconfiguration of party leadership and a more fragmented States-General. The country has increasingly positioned itself within EU and NATO frameworks, publishing a 2023 Security Strategy and continuing to emphasize defense, resilience, and development aid as core elements of its foreign and security policy. Social debates intensified around immigration and integration, with populist and anti-immigration voices gaining prominence and shaping parliamentary dynamics in the mid-2020s. Economically, the Netherlands sustained substantial official development assistance and a pro-growth policy environment while balancing domestic reforms and nitrogen/emission challenges that have affected housing and construction policies. Internationally, the Netherlands has continued to advocate for robust European defense collaboration, humanitarian aid, and multilateral engagement, hosting and contributing to NATO and EU initiatives even as national politics grew more complex and polarized.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2018, three independence referendums under the Nouméa Accord have all rejected independence, with the 2021 vote showing an overwhelming ‘no’ alongside a relatively low turnout, signaling the persistence of ties to France despite rising pro-independence energy. In parallel, a pro‑independence bloc gained a majority in New Caledonia’s Congress in 2021, marking a shift in local governance though not a move toward immediate independence. Debates over self‑determination and possible electorate expansion have kept constitutional and political discussions ongoing, even as participation rules and referendum terms have remained controversial. The Covid‑19 pandemic disrupted the referendum schedule and highlighted social and regional disparities, complicating political calculations and policy priorities. France has continued to back a negotiated, gradual path within its special status for New Caledonia, with international observers noting durable security and stability alongside persistent political frictions over the territory’s future.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2017, New Zealand has operated under a Labour-led government formed through a coalition and confidence arrangements, pursuing social reforms, climate action, and regional development while managing constrained public finances. The administration has prioritized social equity and Pacific resilience, expanding health reforms and instituting new recognitions like Matariki as a public holiday, alongside ongoing investments in research and development. Foreign policy has shifted toward more active Pacific diplomacy, sanctions on Russia after the Ukraine invasion, new free-trade commitments with the UK and the EU, and careful balancing of relations with China and the United States. The economy confronted post-pandemic headwinds with higher interest rates and housing challenges, even as migration fueled population resilience and policy moves such as carbon and transport reforms reoriented consumer and business incentives. By the mid-2020s New Zealand positioned itself as a climate-conscious middle power focused on regional security, climate finance, and governance debates around Treaty obligations and Māori participation in policy design.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2014, Daniel Ortega’s government in Nicaragua has steadily centralized power, culminating in a brutal 2018 crackdown on protests that left hundreds dead and led to widespread arrests and the seizure of independent media and civil-society groups. In the 2021 general elections, opposition figures faced disqualification and detentions, triggering international criticism of the electoral process and concerns about democratic openness. Human-rights groups and international bodies have repeatedly documented abuses by security forces and pro-government groups, a pattern that has persisted alongside pressure on media and civil society. Economically, Nicaragua has faced governance challenges and mismanagement allegations that have affected investor confidence and longer-term development plans, even as social programs and infrastructure needs remain central to public discourse. International positioning has ranged from condemnation and sanctions by some governments to limited engagement by others, with ongoing debates over how to respond to what many observers describe as a deteriorating democratic space and rule-of-law concerns.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since the July 2023 coup, Niger has been governed by a military junta under Abdourahamane Tchiani, with ECOWAS sanctions and threatened intervention shaping international leverage and regional diplomacy. The security landscape remains dominated by jihadist violence and cross-border spillovers in the Sahel, pressuring the junta to balance counterterrorism with regional cooperation and domestic stability. The political crisis and security challenges have also affected governance and civil liberties, including detentions and contested transitions as the regime proclaims a multi-year roadmap. Niger’s economy remains highly dependent on external partners and mineral revenues, with recent moves toward reshaping the uranium sector, including discussions of nationalizing key assets and diversifying away from commodity dependence. International positioning has seen Niger recalibrate ties among France, the United States, regional blocs, and new partners like Algeria and other Sahel actors amid a broader shift away from Western military presences in the region.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2015, Nigeria’s democratic trajectory has centered on Buhari’s presidency with promises on security, anti-corruption, and economic reforms, shaping a more centralized governance approach at the federal level. The security landscape remained volatile, with Boko Haram’s insurgency receding in some years but banditry, farmer-herder clashes, and secessionist tensions continuing, prompting sustained military and regional cooperation. The 2020 EndSARS protests mobilized Nigeria’s youth and altered political engagement, influencing discourse and voting patterns visible in the 2023 general elections. Economically, Nigeria faced recessions and inflation pressures while pursuing diversification, infrastructure, and public finance reforms, with some governance achievements noted but growth not the main focus for general readers. Internationally, Nigeria positioned itself as a security and economic partner in Africa and with Western and regional institutions, seeking support and collaboration in counter-terrorism and development efforts.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: North Korea conducted a sustained sprint of nuclear and missile testing through 2016–2017, signaling a rapid hardening of its deterrent capabilities and triggering intensified international sanctions and security concerns; after peaking in 2017, Pyongyang shifted to diplomacy in 2018–2019, holding summits with South Korea and the United States that produced high-profile rhetoric but limited verifiable denuclearization steps; the 2020s brought renewed sanctions and periodic testing while the regime prioritized strategic weapons development amid the global pandemic and economic strain, dampening any substantial growth in the domestic economy; security doctrine has continued to emphasize self-reliance and military readiness, with Pyongyang signaling a willingness to use deterrence to extract concessions in diplomacy; by 2025–2026, North Korea maintained parallel channels with Beijing and Moscow while cautiously engaging some partners and reaffirming its nuclear status, navigating a multipolar international landscape with limited, but ongoing, diplomacy alongside persistent coercive pressure from the United States and its allies.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since taking office in October 2021, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre leads a minority Labour–Centre Party government that has pursued a more consultative, reform-minded approach while navigating a divided Storting and ongoing debates over EU energy policy and welfare reform. Norway has reinforced its security posture as a steadfast NATO ally on its northern flank, prioritizing Arctic deterrence and alliance cooperation amid increased regional activity, including new Arctic-focused NATO initiatives in 2024–2026. Socially, Norway has continued to integrate migrant and refugee communities while advancing expansive gender-equality policies and debates over social cohesion, with evolving public discourse on welfare state sustainability. Economically, the country has kept steering its sovereign wealth fund toward diversified, greener investments and reduced exposure to oil-sector volatility, even as oil and gas remain important export sources and a subject of domestic policy discussions. Internationally, Norway has positioned itself as a pragmatic mediator and green energy partner, balancing close Atlantic ties with Nordic cooperation and a proactive stance in Arctic governance and global climate diplomacy.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Haitham bin Tariq became Oman’s sultan in January 2020, inheriting a transition that has sought continuity in foreign policy while pursuing gradual domestic reforms under Vision 2040. The 2020s have tested Oman with the COVID-19 pandemic and oil-price volatility, prompting fiscal adjustment and continued state-led development despite slower growth in the nonhydrocarbon sector. Governance moves, including formalizing line of succession and cabinet appointments, have aimed to improve policy predictability and implementation. Oman’s diversification push—articulated in Vision 2040 and its five-year plans—seeks to raise private-sector share of the economy and broaden nonoil activity through investment and reform, though progress remains uneven. diplomatically, Muscat has sought to balance regional powers and maintain steady ties with the United States, Saudi Arabia, Iran, and other partners, reinforcing its image as a pragmatic regional intermediary.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2016, Pakistan’s political landscape has seen civilian governments navigate a powerful military establishment’s influence, with a formal transition of power occurring after the 2018 elections and again after the 2024 vote, shaping governance and policy continuity amid instability. Security remained volatile as the northwestern insurgencies and Baluch nationalist violence persisted, contributing to spikes in militant attacks and casualties through 2024 and beyond, even as military operations expanded to counter them. Social and political currents included protests over governance, demands for accountability, and debates over media and internet freedom, all occurring within a system of multiparty competition and shifting coalitions at national and provincial levels. Economically, Pakistan engaged with the International Monetary Fund through a multi-year program beginning in 2019, accompanied by structural reforms and fiscal measures intended to stabilize external financing, tax collection, and public spending while seeking to protect vulnerable populations; the program has shaped policies through multiple reviews and extensions up to 2024–2025. Internationally, Pakistan sought to maintain and recalibrate its regional role, balancing security considerations with growing emphasis on regional connectivity projects under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor and adjusting diplomacy amid evolving ties with neighboring states, while facing climate-related shocks such as floods that intensified fiscal and development pressures.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2016, the Palestinian political landscape has been defined by ongoing competition between the Fatah-led Palestinian Authority in the West Bank and Hamas in Gaza, punctuated by periodic reconciliation talks that have yet to translate into durable unity. Security and governance arrangements remained fractured, with movement and access constraints shaping everyday life and governance in both territories. In the 2020s, renewed but fragile reconciliation efforts surfaced, alongside continued international engagement over Palestinian statehood, security, and governance amid shifting regional dynamics. The October 2023 Hamas attack and the ensuing Gaza war deepened Palestinian internal debates about unity and reconstruction, while also intensifying international focus on humanitarian relief and accountability for aid and reconstruction planning. By 2024–2025, the Palestinian economy faced a severe downturn driven by conflict, blockade effects, and volatile aid flows, with unemployment high and donor funding uneven, even as some pockets of recovery emerged in the West Bank alongside Gaza’s ongoing humanitarian crisis.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, Panama’s political scene has shifted from the end of Cortizo’s presidency toward a more fragmented coalition after the 2024 elections, complicating governance and policy continuity. Security and rule-of-law efforts have deepened through international cooperation, including Interpol-led capacity building and the establishment of a Border Information and Analysis Targeting Unit to disrupt transnational crime. Social dynamics have been marked by persistent inequality, student and worker protests, and large migrant movements through Darién in 2023, underscoring demands for inclusion and public accountability. The economy remains highly linked to logistics and canal activity, with major infrastructure projects expanding capacity and connectivity, even as the pandemic underscored the need for diversification and resilience. Panama has sought to recalibrate its international posture by balancing ties with China and traditional partners, exemplified by the 2024 arrival of a new Chinese ambassador and ongoing dialogue about the canal’s strategic role in regional trade.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since James Marape took office in 2019, Papua New Guinea has pursued reforms aimed at governance, public service capacity, and diversifying the economy beyond resource-led growth, while facing ongoing corruption and fiscal pressures. In 2022 PNG held a general election that reinforced a relatively stable political trajectory and led to continued parliamentary reshaping, with new district arrangements approved in 2022 and implemented in subsequent years. Security and border management remained a persistent focus, including maritime policing and efforts to strengthen state authority across the country and its vast EEZ and land border with Indonesia. International positioning has grown through deliberate policy actions, most notably the March 2026 Foreign Policy White Paper that outlines PNG’s strategic direction and its theme of balancing security with development, as part of a broader long-term national agenda. Social and humanitarian issues, including the 2017 shutdown of Manus Island detention facilities, continue to shape PNG’s domestic policy and its relations with Australia and multilateral partners in addressing refugee and human rights concerns.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Paraguay’s political landscape shifted markedly after 2008, when the Colorado Party lost power for the first time in decades to a center-left coalition led by Fernando Lugo, signaling a competitive multi-party system that continued with Horacio Cartes’s presidential win in 2013 and a subsequent shift to President Santiago Peña in 2023. The security arena has featured persistent crime and organized crime dynamics, including cross-border drug networks and high-profile investigations that drew international attention and occasional tensions with partners such as the United States, especially around sanctions related to illicit activity seen in 2024. Social and development policy has focused on expanding social protection, education, and human capital under national development plans, while emphasizing resilience to inequality and urbanization pressures, with international financial institutions stressing inclusive growth. Paraguay’s economy remains heavily tied to agricultural exports and natural resources, complemented by ongoing reforms and an open trade regime that the World Bank and OECD have highlighted as drivers of progress while warning about vulnerability to external shocks and climate risks. In foreign policy, Paraguay has sought broader regional integration through Mercosur while also pursuing diversified international ties and a more institutionalized approach to governance and rule of law, reflecting a gradual move away from centralized patronage toward more transparent political processes, albeit with continued scrutiny from watchdog groups.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: In December 2022, after Pedro Castillo was removed from office, Dina Boluarte became Peru’s president, igniting widespread demonstrations that highlighted long‑standing grievances over political corruption, congressional volatility, and regional disparities. Security concerns rose as protests intensified in 2022–2023, with multiple deadly episodes and widespread accusations of excessive force by police and military, drawing international scrutiny. Social change manifested in sustained mobilizations by Indigenous and rural communities demanding fairness, representation, and early elections, reshaping Peru’s political discourse even as protests fluctuated in intensity through 2023 and into 2024. Economically, the country confronted inflation and sluggish growth linked to the post‑pandemic environment, with poverty and inequality persisting as central, not merely macro growth statistics. Peru’s international positioning showed cautious engagement with regional partners and the wider world as it navigated governance crises at home while maintaining diplomatic relations and trade interests.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since Rodrigo Duterte took office in 2016, the Philippines pursued a hard-edged domestic security campaign, notably its drug war, which drew international scrutiny while reshaping law enforcement and civil liberties debates. Duterte also imposed martial law in Mindanao in 2017 to confront Islamist militants, a policy extended through 2019 and shaping security dynamics in the south. In foreign policy, his administration courted China economically and diplomatically while keeping formal ties with allies, and the country withdrew from the ICC in 2019, signaling a shift in its international legal stance; later, President Marcos Jr. moved toward a more balanced, if cautious, posture in the region, reasserting traditional ties with the United States alongside growing engagement with China and regional partners. The economy saw a push to attract Chinese investments and energy ventures, even as the country continued arbitration-era disputes in the South China Sea and faced domestic social changes, including political realignments and debates over governance, accountability, and corruption.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2015, Poland’s ruling Law and Justice party pushed sweeping reforms to the judiciary and other institutions, triggering long-running disputes with Brussels over rule of law and EU standards. The European Commission and European Court of Justice repeatedly challenged these reforms, leading to infringement proceedings and, in several cases, rulings that limited or questioned the government’s moves while negotiations over EU funds continued. In 2024 and 2025 a new government coalition under Donald Tusk signaled a recalibration toward closer EU alignment and engagement with EU institutions, including a plan to restore judicial independence and secure recovery funds; the Article 7 procedure was formally closed but EU-Poland tensions lingered in other areas. On security and foreign policy, Poland reinforced its NATO role and supported Ukraine’s defense, while maintaining a robust stance on defense spending and deterrence, even as domestic debates about national sovereignty persisted. Socially, Poland saw ongoing clashes over reproductive rights and LGBT rights, with activism and legal challenges highlighting deep societal cleavages, even as new civil partnerships and reforms entered public discussion.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: From 2015/2016 onward, a Socialist-led government and left-wing support reversed austerity measures and expanded social policy, reshaping the welfare state. Portugal reinforced its security and international role, increasing defense spending and contributing to NATO missions while hosting discussions on EU security funding. Economically, the country benefited from EU funds, tourism and exports, helping growth rebound in 2023-2024 while keeping living costs in check. Social change included debates on housing and rental stock, with continued emphasis on social inclusion and energy transition, including renewables and electric mobility. International positioning saw Portugal strengthening ties within the EU and NATO, while pursuing diversification in energy and strategic industries such as lithium and green hydrogen.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Puerto Rico faced a defining fiscal confrontation after PROMESA was enacted in 2016 to restructure its debt under a U.S. oversight board, shaping political dynamics around governance and fiscal responsibility for years to come. The 2017 Hurricane Maria disaster exposed and accelerated infrastructure vulnerabilities, prompting a long recovery process that highlighted energy, housing, and public-service resilience challenges. In recent politics, new coalitions and debates over status options have continued to test Puerto Rico’s traditional two-party system, including participation in 2020 status discussions and related political discourse. The island’s economy has pursued diversification and reconstruction efforts within a federal framework, with ongoing attention to debt restructuring, public-utility reform, and investment in social programs rather than focusing solely on growth metrics. International positioning has trended toward greater visibility in policy dialogue with Washington and engagement in resilience planning, development aid, and disaster preparedness initiatives.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: From 2017 onward, Qatar navigated the Gulf crisis by maintaining an open foreign policy and gradually restoring regional ties after a three-and-a-half-year blockade ended in 2021, signaling a recalibration of its regional stance; it also deepened security and diplomatic engagement with Western partners, including the United States. Its international posture emphasized mediation and balance, with Qatar playing a more active role in Gulf diplomacy and broader regional discussions despite ongoing tensions with some neighbors. The 2022 FIFA World Cup and massive preparatory investments accelerated non-hydrocarbon activity and underscored a long-running diversification push under the Qatar National Vision 2030, with the Third National Development Strategy launched in 2024 guiding medium-term priorities. Qatar has explicitly linked diversification to sustainable development, seeking to broaden the economy beyond hydrocarbons through targeted sectors and private-sector growth, while leveraging its energy position to finance development and regional diplomacy. Throughout this period, Qatar sought to position itself as a regional hub for energy, finance, and mediation, balancing relations with Gulf neighbors, the United States, and other major powers to preserve influence and security.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Romania has seen prolonged political volatility since 2019, with coalition shifts and protests over corruption reforms that culminated in 2021 and continued into the 2020s, shaping governance and public trust. The country has reinforced its security role as a NATO member, hosting expansive military infrastructure and debating defense spending targets while balancing regional deterrence with alliance commitments. Social strains surfaced through teacher, healthcare, and other public-sector protests in 2023–2024, reflecting discontent with budget priorities and governance amid a pro-European coalition. The economy benefited from EU funds and structural investment even as fiscal deficits and political turbulence complicated reforms and debt management. Throughout the period, Romania maintained a pro-Western posture—anchored in the EU and NATO—while facing concerns about domestic governance and external pressures, including Russian influence and regional security dynamics.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, Russia centralized political power under Vladimir Putin while formal constitutional and institutional changes in 2020 reinforced term limits in theory but preserved long‑running leadership in practice. In 2022 Moscow launched a full‑scale invasion of Ukraine, triggering sweeping sanctions, a war‑driven shift to a defense‑heavy economy, and deepening estrangement from the West. Domestically, social and economic controls intensified, with state media and security services playing a key role in managing dissent and shaping public narratives during a period of economic pressure and rising state mobilization. Internationally, Russia pivoted toward closer alignment with the Global South and partners such as China, while using its wartime budget to sustain military and strategic ambitions amid sanctions and currency pressures. The combination of sanctions, increased military spending, and diplomatic realignment has reshaped Moscow’s security posture and its engagement with global institutions, even as ordinary Russians face inflation, limited growth opportunities, and tighter social controls.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade Rwanda under President Paul Kagame has maintained political stability while tightening space for opposition and dissent, with tightly managed elections in 2017 and 2024 that drew concerns about political freedoms. Security policy has remained assertive and highly centralized, with Kigali portraying its approach as essential for regional stability in the Great Lakes, amid ongoing regional security engagements. Social transformation continued apace through improvements in health, education, and social protection programs aimed at cohesion and resilience, even as social discourse and civil society engagement remained constrained. Economically, Rwanda pursued diversification and private-sector development under Vision 2050, building on Vision 2020 groundwork to aim for upper‑middle income status by 2035 and greater infrastructure and productivity gains. Internationally, Kigali continued to cultivate relationships across Africa and with Western partners, leveraging its development narrative while facing scrutiny over governance and rights from human rights monitors and watchdogs.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2016 South Sudan has been in a phased peace process that culminated in the 2018 Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict (R-ARCSS) and the 2020 formation of the Revitalized Transitional Government of National Unity, an arrangement designed to unite the main factions for a 36‑month transition toward elections. The security landscape remained volatile, with periodic clashes and ongoing efforts to deploy unified forces under regional and international mechanisms, even as some violence subsided after the 2018 accord. Socially, the country continued to grapple with displacement and humanitarian needs while authorities urged refugees and residents to return home, signaling a fragile but ongoing stabilization effort. Economically, oil production dominates revenue but governance fragility and uneven implementation of peace commitments have constrained broad development and investment. Internationally, South Sudan has remained a focal point of IGAD and U.S./EU diplomacy, with sanctions and peace‑process diplomacy shaping its regional and global positioning.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Mohammed bin Salman’s accession and the 2016 launch of Vision 2030 have driven a broad economic and social reform agenda aimed at reducing dependence on oil and expanding private-sector activity. The kingdom introduced social liberalization measures—opening cinemas, expanding entertainment, and allowing women to drive—alongside fiscal changes like VAT to fund diversification. Since 2015, Saudi policy in Yemen has become more security-focused, heightening regional tensions and humanitarian concerns while reinforcing a more assertive regional posture. Analysts have praised progress on modernization and private-sector development but also cautioned about uneven reforms, governance bottlenecks, and the limits of political liberalization.
