International positioning has increasingly centered on grand-scale investments, global sport and cultural engagements, and a push to redefine Saudi Arabia’s role in regional security and global markets, even as domestic reform debates continue to unfold.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Senegal held the March 2024 presidential election, resulting in Bassirou Diomaye Faye becoming the youngest president in the country’s history and signaling a continued but contested evolution of its democratic system. Security-wise, the country has remained comparatively stable in a volatile Sahel, with experts stressing that Senegal has not suffered major jihadist attacks while authorities emphasize prevention and resilience. Socially, journalists and civil society have faced increasing security risks amid regional instability, raising concerns about press freedom and public discourse. Economically, the country has pressed on with diversification and development projects, even as observers caution that growth does not automatically translate into broad improvements and highlight ongoing debt and fiscal pressures. Internationally, Senegal has sought to maintain regional leadership within ECOWAS and leverage its diplomatic ties, including outreach to regional leaders amid regional coups, while continuing to position itself as a stabilizing partner in West Africa.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Serbia’s political trajectory since 2014 has been dominated by the consolidation of power under President Aleksandar Vučić and the SNS, with growing centralization and concerns over media pluralism and the rule of law affecting EU credibility. payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Julius Maada Bio and his SLPP government won the 2018 presidential and parliamentary elections, steering Sierra Leone toward governance reforms and anti-corruption efforts while facing the challenge of stabilizing public trust. The country recovered from the 2014–15 Ebola outbreak, being declared Ebola-free by 2016, which helped political normalcy but underscored ongoing social resilience needs. Security governance and post‑conflict reforms have continued with international support as the state strengthens health systems, the rule of law, and civilian oversight after past crises. Economically, Sierra Leone remains resource-rich but volatile, with mining-driven growth and a push from international partners to improve debt sustainability, revenue management, and macro-fiscal stability through 2024 and beyond. Internationally, the authorities have deepened engagement with the IMF and World Bank, aligning the National Development Plan 2024–2030 with reforms to governance, finance, and development to sustain inclusive progress.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Slovakia’s politics were jolted by mass protests in 2018 following the Jan Kuciak murder, prompting government reshuffles and contributing to the end of Robert Fico’s then-dominant coalition; since then the country has pursued greater EU and NATO alignment while grappling with corruption watchdog reforms and a shifting party system. The 2020s saw Slovakia deepen its ties with European security architecture, including continued participation in NATO’s eastern flank arrangements and a focus on defence modernization. The government framework has repeatedly turned on coalition dynamics and public debates over media freedom, anti-corruption probes, and judicial reform, with high-profile political violence in 2024 underscoring fragility at the top. At the same time, Slovakia has leveraged EU Recovery and Resilience funds to support green and digital transitions, urban development, and social infrastructure, while maintaining a strong industrial base tied to the automotive sector and benefiting from EU funds for investment. International positioning has grown more pragmatic, balancing Western alliance commitments with regional diplomacy and responding to energy and supply-chain pressures affecting growth and reform trajectories.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: After a period of political volatility, Robert Golob and his Freedom Movement formed the government following Slovenia’s 2022 parliamentary election, with his cabinet approved in late May 2022. The Golob administration aligned Slovenia more closely with EU and NATO priorities, engaging in high-level security diplomacy and shaping policies under the EU’s framework and NATO commitments. Public support for the government fluctuated, with analyses noting a decline in approval by late 2023 as the administration navigated domestic challenges. Slovenia continued to anchor its security and foreign policy within NATO and EU structures, emphasizing collective defence, crisis management, and multilateral cooperation. By March 2026, elections again reshaped the political landscape, highlighting ongoing contention between liberal and conservative camps and signaling continued volatility in Slovenia’s political trajectory.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, the Solomon Islands shifted from its traditional security reliance on Australia toward a more assertive alignment with China, culminating in a 2022 security pact that alarmed the United States and its allies about potential Chinese security access in the region. In 2023 the government expanded security cooperation with China through a policing pact, signaling deeper security ties beyond the original agreement. Domestically, Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare steered a fragile, multi-party coalition through the 2021 riots and ongoing constitutional tensions, while Malaita province pushed for greater autonomy. Internationally, U.S. and Australian diplomacy intensified as Washington reopened its embassy in 2023 and regional partners sought to balance Beijing’s influence in the Pacific. Economically, the Solomons pursued diversification and development with a focus on investment climate and social outcomes rather than chasing high GDP growth alone.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Somalia has gradually rebuilt a federal system since the 2012 transition, with the 2016 electoral process and 2021 indirect presidential vote reflecting uneven state-building amid continuing political competition and security concerns. The insurgency of al-Shabaab remains a major security challenge, though Somali forces backed by international partners have pursued offensives and seen the transfer of security responsibilities from AMISOM to ATMIS in the mid-2020s. Social and development dynamics have been shaped by COVID-19 disruptions, humanitarian needs, and reform efforts aimed at institutions and public services, even as progress on fiscal and governance reform remains uneven. International engagement has endured, with sustained security cooperation, aid, and financing while Somalia 6 that international creditors and donors have sought clearer governance and budgetary reform paths. By the mid-2020s, Somalia’s government emphasizes security sector reform, institutional building, and development plans like the National Transformation Plan to attract investment and guide state-building, even as regional and clan dynamics continue to complicate federal-state power sharing.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, Somaliland has steadily deepened its devolved governance model, holding elections and pursuing governance reforms while remaining unrecognized by the international community. Security challenges have tested stability, notably the 2023–2024 Las Anod clashes between Somaliland forces and Dhulbahante fighters that raised concerns about territorial control and mediation mechanisms. Social and economic change has been driven by diaspora-backed development and investment in infrastructure, with Berbera port expanding trade and broader diversification of the economy beyond livestock alone. Despite improvements in institutions and public services, external aid remains constrained by non-recognition, shaping how international partners engage and fund development. In 2025–2026, Somaliland’s push for recognition intensified, including high-level diplomatic activity and landmark discussions around formal recognition by states such as Israel, reshaping regional dynamics and sparking debate about Somalia’s sovereignty and regional security commitments.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2018 South Africa has pursued anti-corruption reforms after the State Capture Inquiry exposed extensive graft, with Ramaphosa’s administration releasing progress reports on implementing those recommendations and pursuing accountability through units like the SIU and Asset Forfeiture Unit. The energy crisis has driven a shift toward unbundling Eskom and expanding private generation under a National Transmission Company framework and the Just Energy Transition plan, features highlighted in OECD and World Economic Forum analyses as key to stabilizing supply and enabling investment. The 2024 elections fragmented the ANC’s parliamentary majority, leading to a coalition government and renewed scrutiny over governance, ethics, and Ramaphosa’s leadership amid ongoing corruption allegations related to the Phala Phala matter. South Africa has positioned itself as an active participant in global energy and economic transition initiatives, including a targeted energy transition investment plan and international partnerships aimed at financing decarbonization and infrastructure modernization. Internationally, Pretoria has sought to balance domestic reform with regional diplomacy and governance, aiming to strengthen procurement transparency and governance institutions while maintaining a role in multilateral forums and regional security efforts.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: South Korea’s political trajectory over the past decade has seen a shift from Moon Jae-in’s liberal governance (2017–2022) toward a more hard-edged, security-focused stance under President Yoon Suk Yeol (2022–present), with policy emphasis on alliance reliability and deterrence against North Korea’s nuclear threats; the country has pursued a cautious but persistent engagement strategy toward Pyongyang while restoring military trust and seeking pragmatic security deals. South Korea’s security environment has been dominated by North Korea’s evolving capabilities and periodic inter-Korean outreach, including restored but fragile communication lines and periodic tensions around missile tests and space launches, alongside ongoing U.S.–ROK security cooperation and allied exercises. Social change has expanded into public debate over gender, equality, and minority rights, highlighted by broad civic activism and the emergence of movements that challenge traditional norms, even as the government navigates competing cultural tensions and policy shifts. Economically, the country has remained heavily reliant on semiconductor exports and IT manufacturing, while seeking broader diversification of exports and industrial policy to reduce over-reliance on a few sectors, and the government has announced growth strategies and export initiatives to sustain momentum into the mid-2020s. Internationally, Seoul has balanced a hedging strategy between the United States and China, pursued a proactive Indo-Pacific posture, deepened regional ties with like-minded partners, and aimed to strengthen multilateral engagement, including through regional trade and security coalitions, while pressing for stable diplomacy with neighbors and partners alike.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: The PSOE-led government under Pedro Sánchez has steered Spain through the tail end of the Catalan autonomy crisis and broader political realignments, including growth of new party dynamics on the left and right. In 2024, parliament approved a controversial amnesty to address Catalonia’s separatist actions, a move seen as essential for restoring political stability but also drawing domestic debate. Spain’s Recovery and Resilience Plan, accompanied by labor-market reforms, aims to curb temporary contracting and enhance active policies and skills training, shaping the country’s employment landscape. The period has also seen social policy gains, including gradual rises in the minimum wage and improved social protection, alongside a recovery from pandemic-era economic shocks. Internationally, Spain has continued to position itself as an active EU partner, leveraging EU funds and maintaining roles in European security and diplomacy amid domestic political shifts.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Sri Lanka faced a sovereign debt crunch starting in 2016, prompting IMF engagement and tax reform efforts as the island sought external financing while navigating a fragile political landscape that culminated in a Rajapaksa-led government return in 2019 and a shift toward closer ties with China alongside traditional partners like India. The Easter Sunday bombings in 2019 exposed security gaps, led to emergency measures and a broad push to strengthen counterterrorism laws and surveillance, and energized public debate about accountability for security agencies. Social tensions rose in the wake of the attacks, including anti-Muslim incidents and debate over minority rights, even as the country pursued stabilization and reforms under new governance structures. By the early 2020s Sri Lanka pursued economic stabilization with foreign support, including an IMF program and debt management steps, while also strengthening international engagement and development financing to support resilience, tourism recovery, and social indicators beyond headline growth figures.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since Omar al-Bashir’s removal in 2019, Sudan pursued a transitional civilian-led government but faced a 2021 military coup that halted the transfer of power and sparked ongoing protests and political friction. The country’s security situation deteriorated in Darfur and other regions as clashes between military and paramilitary forces intensified, displacing civilians and aggravating a broad humanitarian crisis. In 2020 Sudan was removed from the U.S. list of state sponsors of terrorism, a move that opened doors to international loans and engagement, while debt-relief prospects and IMF/World Bank support remained conditional on progress in governance and peace. Economic conditions have remained fragile, with episodes of contraction in 2020 and a broader push for debt relief and resumed access to international finance as Sudan slowly reintegrated with the global system. International positioning has involved signaling normalization with Israel as part of broader diplomacy, even as Western governments pressed Khartoum to sustain a civilian-led transition and resolve institutional stalemate after the coup.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Chandrikapersad Santokhi, elected president in 2020, steered Suriname through a programme of governance reform and anti-corruption measures after years of political tension linked to the Bouterse era. The government formed a broad coalition and pursued constitutional and judicial accountability, including the 1982 killings investigations that culminated in post‑2020 prosecutions and trials. Security and rule-of-law challenges persisted as crime and illicit networks drew scrutiny, even as civilian authorities asserted greater control over security forces. The economy shifted toward a resource‑based outlook with renewed emphasis on oil and gold development, supported by IMF‑backed stabilization efforts and investor focus on offshore oil prospects while aspiring to diversify away from commodity dependence. International partners—ranging from the IMF and World Bank to regional bodies and OAS—pressed Suriname to strengthen governance, transparency, and macroeconomic sustainability ahead of expected oil-driven growth.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: From 2014 onward, the Social Democrats governed Sweden with coalition partners, a period that ended after the 2022 election when a center-right bloc led by Ulf Kristersson formed a minority government with support from the Sweden Democrats. The Tidö Agreement codified this arrangement and steered a security- and migration-focused policy agenda, broadening collaboration with other parties while keeping the SD out of the cabinet. Sweden formally applied to join NATO after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and became a full member in March 2024, marking a major shift in its international security posture. In domestic policy, the government highlighted immigration and integration challenges, urban inequality, and crime prevention, seeking structural reforms to neighborhoods identified as most affected. Economically, Sweden continued its EU integration trajectory and relied on EU-level frameworks and surveillance analyses to shape growth and resilience without emphasizing GDP alone.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Switzerland has continued to pursue a pragmatic, multilateral and bilateral approach to international relations, reinforcing its role as a neutral but globally connected actor. The 2020–23 Foreign Policy Strategy prioritized peace and security, sustainable development, and digitalisation while emphasising cooperation within multilateral institutions and with partners beyond Europe. In 2021 the Federal Council assessed alternatives to the EU institutional agreement and ultimately chose to maintain a robust Bilateral I/II framework with the EU, reinforcing cooperation on migration, research, and the internal market without full institutional union. Swiss security policy has sought to balance neutrality with increased international cooperation, aligning military, intelligence, and civil protection efforts to respond to evolving security challenges. Domestically, Switzerland faced social and political debates over immigration and social policy, while its economy remained highly responsive to global innovation networks and foreign engagement through bilateral channels and international organisations.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since December 2024, Syria has entered a transitional period led by Ahmad al-Sharaa that marks the formal end of the Assad regime and initiates efforts to rebuild state institutions amid ongoing security challenges. Clashes and shifting control in 2025–2026 have seen renewed fighting and fragile ceasefires, even as government forces push to reestablish authority in former opposition areas and Kurdish-led zones seek stabilizing arrangements. Internationally, there has been growing attention to reconstruction and diplomacy alongside debates over sanctions, with some discussions about rolling back punitive measures to facilitate stability and investment. Human rights and humanitarian concerns persist, including reports of abuses and ongoing displacement, which complicate prospects for social reconciliation in a war-weary society. Economic and development prospects increasingly hinge on credible governance, security, and inclusive policies that can attract investment and support from global partners.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2016, Taiwan’s political trajectory has been defined by the ruling DPP’s push for stronger democratic resilience amid intensified pressure from Beijing and reduced formal international space, even as Taipei sought to bolster domestic institutions and security capabilities. The 2016 and 2020 elections reinforced a preference for the status quo in cross-strait relations, while economic strategy shifted toward supply-chain resilience and diversification beyond China, notably in semiconductors and tech services. In 2024, Lai Ching-te’s presidency and broader cross-strait policy debates highlighted a cautious approach to independence, continued U.S.-Taiwan engagements, and efforts to sustain regional partnerships, even as China escalated military signaling. Domestic politics shifted with the emergence of centrist and reform-minded forces, such as the Taiwan People’s Party, influencing governance norms, recall politics, and electoral strategy ahead of local and national contests. By the mid-2020s, Taiwan pursued deeper regional alignments (e.g., Indo-Pacific economic-security initiatives) and sought to strengthen international space through diversified diplomacy and stable defense postures, while maintaining its core commitment to a peaceful, status-quo-based relationship with Beijing.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Tajikistan over the last decade has seen President Emomali Rahmon cement a long tenure following the 2016 constitutional referendum that extended his rule and reshaped political competition. The security landscape has been shaped by persistence of border controls with Afghanistan and ongoing reliance on Moscow-led security arrangements, alongside domestic crackdowns that underscore the regime’s tight political control. Economically, growth has remained resilient in parts of the period, with policy focus on broader development under the National Development Strategy 2030 and ongoing emphasis on improving the investment climate, though private sector investment and diversification remain challenging. Social progress includes notable poverty reduction and continued reliance on remittances, alongside social sector reform efforts aimed at expanding access to services for the poor. Internationally, Tajikistan has navigated closer ties with Russia and participation in regional forums like CSTO and SCO while seeking to attract development finance and technical support from the World Bank and other partners.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: From 2015 to 2021, Tanzania under President John Magufuli pursued large infrastructure programs and a hard line on dissent, while crackdowns on opposition and some civil-society voices drew international concern. After Magufuli’s death in March 2021, Vice President Samia Suluhu Hassan became president, becoming the first woman to hold the post and signaling a shift toward political reform and a more permissive media environment, even as critics warned of ongoing repression. Under Hassan, Tanzania resumed engagement with international financial institutions and donors, and she championed a broader reform agenda and regional leadership, while promising reconciliation and rebuilding the political space. Zanzibar-related political tensions and episodes of violence around elections remained a concern, with human-rights groups documenting suppression of opposition and press freedoms in the broader union context. The economy continued to diversify with emphasis on manufacturing, services, and natural-resource projects, and the government pursued mid- to long-term development planning such as Vision 2050, seeking inclusive growth and resilience rather than relying solely on headline growth figures.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since the 2014 coup, Thailand’s political environment has been shaped by the military-led authorities, a new constitution, and a gradual transition toward civilian government, with power often retained by the establishment and the monarchy. The 2019 general election was the first since the coup, but skeptics noted that the military and elite networks still heavily influenced coalition politics and policy direction. The 2020–2021 pro-democracy wave underscored rising social mobilization and calls for constitutional reform, testing the resilience of the post-coup political settlement and highlighting broader questions about governance. Economically, Bangkok’s leadership placed renewed emphasis on the Eastern Economic Corridor to diversify away from reliance on tourism, pairing massive infrastructure with innovation and digital ambitions to spur value-based growth. In international terms, Thailand has sought to position the EEC as a regional hub, supported by foreign-financed projects and development loans in the mid-2020s as part of a broader push to integrate into global supply chains and ASEAN frameworks.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Timor-Leste has enjoyed relatively steady coalition politics since 2016, with the government surviving a mid-2020 reshuffle and parliamentary elections in 2023/24 being validated, signaling resilient but evolving political institutions. Security reform has continued, focusing on professionalizing the police and defence forces and incorporating gender considerations as part of broader SSR efforts. Social development priorities have shifted toward improved service delivery and governance capacity while relying on a future-oriented but still oil-dependent economy, with revenue management and fiscal sustainability gaining emphasis in recent years. The economy remains anchored in oil and gas, with diversification efforts underway around port and infrastructure projects such as Tibar Bay, and ongoing scrutiny of revenue-sharing arrangements with regional partners. Internationally, Timor-Leste has pursued deeper regional engagement—aiming for ASEAN membership and strengthening ties with Australia—while expanding participation in multilateral forums and diversifying its diplomatic and development partnerships.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, Togo has pursued political reform culminating in a 2024 constitutional shift from a presidential to a parliamentary system, a move criticized by opponents as reducing democratic scrutiny while extending governance in practice under President Faure Gnassingbé. The security landscape has absorbed regional spillovers from West Africa’s jihadist and militant threats, with authorities facing attacks and a tightening of security measures domestically ahead of elections. Economically, the country has prioritized transport and energy infrastructure—notably the Lomé port and power projects—while seeking to diversify beyond traditional sectors amid regional integration efforts like AfCFTA, though benefits remain unevenly distributed. Socially, civil society and opposition actors have faced crackdowns and protests have at times intensified, raising concerns about civil liberties and the pace of reform. Internationally, Togo has deepened ties within West Africa and with development partners, emphasizing modernization and private-sector conduits to drive investment and regional connectivity while navigating domestic tensions over governance and term limits.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2015, Trinidad and Tobago’s politics have been dominated by a two‑party dynamic between the PNM and UNC, shaping governance through periodic electoral shifts, coalition dynamics at the local level, and ongoing debates over reform and accountability. The security landscape has deteriorated at times, with the government repeatedly invoking states of emergency to counter gang violence, including a renewed 2026 extension after recent crackdowns and prior measures in 2024–2025. Economically, the country remained heavily energy‑dependent while increasingly pursuing diversification and the growth of non‑energy sectors, with 2022–2024 data showing a rebound in non‑energy activity even as energy revenues remained volatile. Policy efforts to broaden the economy included downstream development, renewable energy pilots, and efforts to attract investment in high‑value exports, alongside a recognition that energy transition would need to accompany growth. Internationally, Trinidad and Tobago has sought to position itself as a regional energy gateway and partner in Caribbean diplomacy, engaging with external partners on LNG, gas fields, and climate and development cooperation.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Kais Saied won Tunisia’s 2019 presidential election and was sworn in in October 2019, positioning himself as an anti‑corruption outsider who would recalibrate the balance of power; his rise coincided with a difficult economic environment and public fatigue with established parties. In July 2021 he froze parliament, dismissed the prime minister, and began ruling by decree, triggering a constitutional crisis that polarized opinion and drew international attention. A July 2022 constitutional referendum backed by Saied’s framework further reshaped the political system, consolidating presidential authority amid a fractured parliament and ongoing street demonstrations. By late 2023 and into 2024, Tunisia’s political trajectory leaned toward stronger executive control, with critics warning of a democratic backslide even as the state argued it was restoring order and tackling corruption. Across these years, the economy and social stresses—unemployment, consumer hardship, and demands for reform—have shaped Tunisia’s international positioning, including repeated IMF talks and engagement with regional and Western partners.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since the mid-2010s, President Erdogan’s AKP has moved toward centralized rule, culminating in a presidential system and tightened control over media and opposition after the 2016 coup attempt. The 2016 attempted coup and the subsequent state of emergency accelerated purges and legal changes that curbed political dissent and reshaped civil society. Economically, Turkey endured high inflation and a shift from unorthodox policy to more orthodox measures after 2023, marked by central-bank policy tightening and a new finance approach. Internationally, Ankara has pursued an assertive, independent foreign policy, deepening ties with Russia and China while trying to manage relations with Europe and the broader region. Socially, the government has faced domestic pushback and warnings about freedom of expression as elections and local governance evolved under tightened political controls.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Turkmenistan largely maintained a personalized autocratic system after Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow's long rule, with formal power transitioning gradually to his son Serdar, who won the 2022 presidential election and took office in March 2022. From 2021 to 2023 the state restructured its legislature, replacing the Halk Maslahaty with a unicameral People’s Council and later appointing the elder Berdimuhamedow as its chairman under the title National Leader. In 2023 the leadership formalized a dynastic consolidation and expanded the elder Berdimuhamedow’s influence, while authorities tightened media and civil-society controls. Economically, Turkmenistan remained heavily dependent on gas exports, with China as a major customer and little diversification in the period, despite occasional state-driven development projects. Internationally, Ashgabat pursued a cautious, status-quo foreign policy, maintaining limited engagement with Western states while expanding energy ties with neighboring and regional partners.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2016, Uganda has remained under Yoweri Museveni and the NRM, with elections that international observers often describe as contested or uneven in their competitive environment; the government has solidified its grip on political space while seeking to modernize governance and security institutions. The 2021 presidential vote was followed by a harsh security crackdown on Bobi Wine and other opponents, drawing widespread criticism over rights abuses and electoral credibility. Social changes include rising youth activism and digital mobilization that challenge the political status quo, even as opposition organizing faces legal and logistical hurdles. Economically, Uganda has pursued infrastructure and development projects financed by a mix of Western aid, development partners, and growing regional and Asian investment, all set against ongoing governance and transparency concerns highlighted by rights groups and foreign observers. Internationally, Kampala has balanced traditional Western partnerships with diversified ties and is navigating regional diplomacy as Museveni signals his intention to seek another term, reflecting a continuity of leadership amid shifting regional dynamics.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2014 Ukraine pivoted from a contentious rapprochement with the EU toward a firmly pro-democracy, Euro-Atlantic trajectory, a shift underscored by Russia's 2014 seizure of Crimea and ongoing conflict in Donbas that culminated in Russia’s full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022. The security landscape has dominated policy, with sustained Western military, financial, and humanitarian support and the rapid evolution of Ukraine’s defense-industrial base as a central pillar of resilience. Politically, Kyiv has pursued governance reforms and closer ties with the EU and NATO, even as reform momentum has faced domestic and external pressures and the security crisis has driven larger strategic realignments. Socially, Ukraine has mobilized civil society, invested in education and reform at the municipal level, and contended with displacement and reconstruction needs amid wartime disruption. International positioning has been shaped by sanctions on Russia, deepening Western coordination, and Ukraine’s enduring pursuit of fuller Euro-Atlantic integration, backed by a broad coalition of partners.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since 2015 the UAE expanded its military footprint in Yemen, deploying ground forces to Aden and pursuing influence in southern Yemen as part of a broader regional security strategy. In 2020 it helped forge the Abraham Accords, normalizing relations with Israel and reshaping its diplomatic and economic outreach beyond the Gulf. Domestically, the leadership under Mohammed bin Zayed has pursued modernization and a security-focused governance model, balancing gradual social liberalization with tight political control. Economically, the UAE has diversified away from hydrocarbons toward finance, logistics, and technology, aiming to cement itself as a regional hub for investment and innovation. Internationally, it has sought to balance relations with major powers, deepen security partnerships, and position itself as a pivotal mediator in regional affairs.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Brexit reshaped UK politics and policy from 2016 onward, driving a realignment of parties, institutions and public debate that the Institute for Government described as the Brexit Effect on government, parliament and politics. Boris Johnson led the country through a tumultuous 2019–2022 period focused on delivering the Brexit deal and navigating constitutional and party fractures, before he resigned in 2022; his era left a lasting imprint on political gridlock and leadership churn. After formal exit, the UK began adjusting to new trade rules with the EU and to a services-led export profile, with official trade data showing services driving growth and goods trade experiencing volatility since 2021, a transition documented by the ONS and related analyses (ONS 2024; Economist Group 2024). Security and strategic posture remained tied to evolving threat assessments, with ongoing updates to the National Security Strategy and related defence reviews guiding mixed budgets and cross-government risk management into the 2020s (GOV.UK NSS/SDSR materials; 2025 NSS). In domestic policy and international positioning, a new Labour government since 2024 has pursued a more unified approach to integrity, immigration policy and Western relations, even as modernization and AI-related disruptions present societal and economic challenges that analysts note as continuing to shape the UK’s trajectory (MusicRadar 2024; OECD/UK trade analyses 2024).

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: The past decade in the United States has been defined by intense political polarization and alternating presidential leadership, shaping policy agendas and public trust. The Biden administration sought to repair alliances, confront China, support Ukraine, and bolster democratic norms, while domestic debates on voting rights and immigration remained contentious. Security policy moved toward strengthening Indo-Pacific commitments, even as later 2026 shifts emerged with debate over multilateral engagement and defense posture in the hemisphere. The economy showed resilience with productivity gains and low unemployment at times, but concerns persisted about debt, inflation, and trade policy effects. International positioning shifted from a more multilateral posture under Biden toward contentious reevaluation of international institutions and alliances in 2025-2026.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, Uruguay sustained a stable democratic system while experiencing a political transition as the Broad Front’s governance gave way to a center‑right coalition led by the National Party around 2025. The government has prioritized tackling organized crime and security cooperation across agencies, signaling a more data‑driven and coordinated approach in the face of evolving crime pressures by 2026. Social policy, notably the 2013 cannabis legalization experiment, has continued to influence public discourse on health, crime, and individual rights while remaining a distinctive feature of Uruguayan policy. Economically, the country moved to address long‑term fiscal solvency through reforms such as the 2023 pension overhaul, with IMF assessments stressing structural reforms to lift potential growth. Internationally, Uruguay advanced its regional and trade positioning, culminating in the 2024 breakthrough toward a Mercosur–European Union framework and an active push to broaden open regionalism beyond the block.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Since Shavkat Mirziyoyev became president in 2016, Uzbekistan has pursued rapid reforms to move from a tightly controlled, state-led economy toward a more market-oriented model, including currency liberalization and extensive judicial and public-sector changes. The government has also expanded international engagement, normalizing ties with neighbors and attracting foreign investment as part of a broader regional diplomacy. Security services were reorganized to reduce state overreach and bolster the rule of law, though experts warn that balancing stability with political openness remains a work in progress. Social reforms included ending compulsory cotton picking and increasing transparency and public governance, with steps like real-time court-trial access and anti-torture measures reported in the late 2010s. By the mid-2020s, Uzbekistan framed development around diversification, regional connectivity, and climate-resilient infrastructure, backed by multilateral partners and development banks.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Vanuatu has experienced sustained political volatility over the past decade, including a 2020–2022 period under Prime Minister Bob Loughman that ended with a snap election and a reshaped parliament. Ishmael Kalsakau then led the country from November 2022 to September 2023 amid intense coalition negotiations and party realignments. The period also featured rapid turnover at the top, with Charlot Salwai returning to office in 2023 and continuing to shape policy through a fragile coalition landscape. The social and development context remained dominated by climate resilience, disaster recovery, and efforts to balance aid-driven development with local governance challenges. In February 2025, Parliament elected Jotham Napat as prime minister, underscoring ongoing fragmentation and the importance of cross-party coalitions in Vanuatu’s international and domestic positioning.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade, Nicolás Maduro’s government has steadily reinforced control, limiting opposition access to elections and using security forces to quell protests. The economy collapsed after the 2014 oil-price shock, with prolonged shortages and hyperinflation that persisted into the 2020s even as global crude prices recovered. Mass emigration grew into a humanitarian crisis, with millions leaving Venezuela while essential services remained strained. Internationally, Venezuela faced sanctions and scrutiny from Western states, while some actors pushed for a monitored transition and credible elections as a path to open markets and repair institutions. By the mid-2020s, observers highlighted political repressions and contested legitimacy around elections, alongside ongoing efforts to negotiate a way forward and to secure relief and investment under international auspices.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: The 2021–2026 leadership cycle in Vietnam saw Nguyen Phu Trong’s extended tenure followed by a January 2026 Party Congress that reinforced a leadership team with a strong security orientation and a push for accelerated governance reform. The 14th National Congress in January 2026 formalized the ascent of To Lam as General Secretary, centralizing power around the security and administrative reform agenda and signaling a decade of policy execution over structural change. Hanoi has moved to broaden its international partnerships, notably establishing a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership with the United States in 2023 to deepen science, technology, and investment links, while balancing relations with major powers. Domestically, Vietnam has pursued sweeping reforms to streamline the public sector, accelerate digital transformation, and modernize the economy, aiming for higher productivity and resilience while maintaining social stability. On security and sovereignty, Vietnam has remained assertive in maritime disputes, working to defend its claims in the South China Sea while expanding maritime diplomacy and regional engagement with ASEAN and other partners.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Over the past decade Western Sahara has seen an enduring standoff between Morocco and the Polisario Front, with a peace process repeatedly stalled despite renewed rounds of talks under UN auspices. The UN peacekeeping mission MINURSO has remained the central international mechanism yet its mandate extension has become a bargaining chip in broader political maneuvering, with a one-year renewal through October 2026 reflecting limited progress toward a mutually acceptable solution. Morocco’s autonomy proposal has gained support from some international actors while remaining opposed by Polisario and its external supporters, contributing to a shifting regional dynamic and Algeria’s ongoing role as a key ally for the Polisario. The regional security situation has become more volatile since the 2020 breakdown of a long-running ceasefire, including sporadic clashes and Moroccan security operations in buffer zones that underscore the fragility of any durable settlement. At the same time, the United States has been actively involved in diplomatic framing—most notably recognizing Morocco’s sovereignty over Western Sahara in 2020 and, more recently, urging a political process and supporting a multiyear MINURSO review, signaling a realignment of international engagement with the conflict.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Yemen’s civil war, which escalated after 2014, has evolved into a multi-sided conflict with sporadic truces and shifting regional alignments, while aid dependence and market fragility constrain recovery. The Houthis have maintained control in much of the north and the capital Sanaa, even as parts of the south have seen power struggles among anti-Houthi forces and regional actors align with different Yemeni factions, including the Southern Transitional Council. In 2024–2025, the World Bank and IMF highlighted severe macroeconomic stress, high inflation, and ongoing humanitarian needs, despite intermittent ceasefires and partial disengagement of some foreign partners. The anti-Houthi coalition’s cohesion has frayed at times as Saudi and UAE interests diverged and new diplomatic efforts sought a pathway to broader peace, with prisoner exchanges and ceasefire pledges shaping the regional calculus. Across society, Yemen’s people continued to face displacement, malnutrition risks, and disrupted services, underscoring the urgency of stabilization and reconstruction alongside international humanitarian assistance.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Zambia entered an IMF-backed reform program in 2020–present to restore fiscal sustainability, restructure external debt, and create room for social spending, with debt restructuring efforts under the G20 Common Framework advancing through 2023–2024; the IMF’s third review in 2024 emphasized continued macroeconomic stabilization, arrears clearance, and governance improvements as prerequisites for more inclusive growth. In 2021, Hakainde Hichilema won the presidency in a competitive, largely peaceful election and has pursued anticorruption measures and public-financial-management reforms aimed at diversifying the economy beyond copper and improving investor confidence. From 2022 into 2024, Zambia formalized debt treatment with official creditors and maintained an outward-facing program to balance social needs with macro stability, while facing drought-driven humanitarian pressures and the need for climate-resilient development. The country has sustained a relatively stable democratic trajectory since 1991, but observers warn that political competition remains intense and that the 2026 electoral cycle could test democratic consolidation amid ongoing economic challenges and regional security dynamics. In 2024, a Constitutional Court ruling regarding former President Edgar Lungu’s eligibility for the 2026 election underscored ongoing political friction surrounding term limits, while public discourse continued to focus on governance, accountability, and the durability of Zambia’s democratic institutions, as documented in election analyses and reputable media.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Zimbabwe’s political trajectory shifted decisively after the 2017 military intervention that ousted Robert Mugabe and propelled Emmerson Mnangagwa into the presidency. In the 2018 general election, Mnangagwa’s ZANU-PF narrowly defeated Nelson Chamisa of the MDC Alliance, amid international attention and ongoing protests over results and governance. The economy has remained volatile, with persistent inflation, currency instability, and debt pressures that have driven engagement with international lenders while limiting broad-based growth. Civil society and opposition voices have faced repression and restrictive governance dynamics, signaling a continuing challenge to political space even as economic stabilization efforts proceed. Internationally, Zimbabwe has sought renewed engagement with institutions such as the IMF and regional bodies, balancing calls for reforms with support for liquidity, governance improvements, and infrastructure investment.

payload.title: Recent history
payload.summary: Eswatini has endured a sustained push for political reform since the 2021 pro-democracy protests, which elicited a violent crackdown by security forces and raised concerns about accountability and human rights. The crisis highlighted the country’s enduring constitutional constraints, with political parties banned since 1973 and the monarchy retaining sweeping power, while international attention and regional mediation efforts sought pathways to dialogue. Social movements, student campaigns, and activist networks pressed for reforms, even as authorities pursued arrests and punitive prosecutions under broad anti-terrorism and sedition laws. Development planning and governance initiatives over the past five years have aimed to address governance, fiscal discipline, and inclusive growth amid drought risk and climate vulnerability, though progress remains uneven. Eswatini has navigated its international positioning through regional bodies and donors while facing ongoing scrutiny from human rights groups and varying levels of external engagement on political reform and rule of law.
